messages.content: I have a customers table and an orders table. How do I list every order together with the name of the customer who placed it, newest first?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id), placed_on TEXT NOT NULL, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'Ana Ruiz'), (2, 'Bo Lind'), (3, 'Cy Park')
SELECT o.id, c.name, o.placed_on, o.total_cents FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id ORDER BY o.placed_on DESC, o.id DESC

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
id	name	placed_on	total_cents
104	Bo Lind	2026-11-09	7300
103	Ana Ruiz	2026-11-09	990
102	Cy Park	2026-11-05	1850
101	Ana Ruiz	2026-11-02	4200

An INNER JOIN pairs each order row with the customer row whose id matches orders.customer_id, and the result has exactly 4 rows - one per order, because every order here has a valid customer. Reading the output top to bottom: order 104 (Bo Lind, 7300 cents) and order 103 share the newest date 2026-11-09, and the id DESC tiebreaker keeps that ordering deterministic instead of leaving the two same-day orders to chance. Two habits to build now: qualify every column with its table alias once two tables are involved, because both tables have an id column and the bare name is ambiguous; and always give ORDER BY a unique final key, because SQL guarantees no order at all without one, and only the prefix order with a non-unique key. The join itself answers 'which customer goes with this order' - it says nothing yet about customers who never ordered, which is where an INNER JOIN quietly stops being the right tool.
Show me every customer and how many orders each has placed - including customers who have never ordered anything.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id), total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'Ana Ruiz'), (2, 'Bo Lind'), (3, 'Cy Park'), (4, 'Dee Osei')
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name ORDER BY order_count DESC, c.name

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	order_count
Ana Ruiz	2
Cy Park	1
Bo Lind	0
Dee Osei	0

The LEFT JOIN keeps all 4 customers, padding the order columns with NULL for anyone without a match, and the counts come out Ana Ruiz: 2, Cy Park: 1, Bo Lind: 0, Dee Osei: 0. Bo Lind and Dee Osei appear with 0 rather than vanishing, which is the entire point of choosing LEFT over INNER here. The detail that makes this work is COUNT(o.id), not COUNT(*): COUNT of a column ignores NULLs, so a padded row contributes 0, while COUNT(*) counts the padded row itself and would report 1 phantom order for every orderless customer. Whenever you aggregate over a LEFT JOIN, count a column from the optional side. GROUP BY c.id (with c.name carried along) rather than by name alone also matters: two different customers can share a name, and grouping by name would merge them into one row with a combined count.
My sales report joins products to order_lines to show units sold per product, but two products from the catalog are missing from the report entirely. Why?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE order_lines (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id), qty INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO products VALUES (1, 'Notebook'), (2, 'Pen'), (3, 'Ruler'), (4, 'Eraser'), (5, 'Stapler')
INSERT INTO order_lines VALUES (11, 1, 3), (12, 1, 2), (13, 3, 5), (14, 5, 1)
SELECT p.name, SUM(l.qty) AS units FROM products p JOIN order_lines l ON l.product_id = p.id GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY p.name
SELECT p.name, COALESCE(SUM(l.qty), 0) AS units FROM products p LEFT JOIN order_lines l ON l.product_id = p.id GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY p.name

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	units
Eraser	0
Notebook	5
Pen	0
Ruler	5
Stapler	1

The report is not broken - the join is doing exactly what an INNER JOIN promises: only pairs that match on both sides survive. Pen and Eraser have no order_lines, so they form no pairs and disappear; the inner version returns 3 rows for a 5-product catalog. The LEFT JOIN version returns all 5 products, with Pen and Eraser showing units of 0 after COALESCE turns their NULL sums into a presentable zero. This is the single most common 'missing rows' bug in reporting SQL: someone writes JOIN meaning 'combine these tables' and the database reads it as 'keep only the overlap'. Decide which side is the population you must never lose - here the catalog - put it on the left, and treat every INNER JOIN in a report as a deliberate filter you should be able to justify, not a default.
I switched my query to a LEFT JOIN so customers without orders would show up, but they still vanish as soon as I add a filter for orders over $50. What is happening?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id), total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'Ana Ruiz'), (2, 'Bo Lind'), (3, 'Cy Park')
SELECT c.name, o.id, o.total_cents FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.total_cents > 5000 ORDER BY c.name

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	id	total_cents
Ana Ruiz	102	8800
Cy Park	103	6100

arguments.sql: SELECT c.name, o.id, o.total_cents FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total_cents > 5000 ORDER BY c.name

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	id	total_cents
Ana Ruiz	102	8800
Bo Lind	NULL	NULL
Cy Park	103	6100

Your WHERE clause is silently converting the LEFT JOIN back into an INNER JOIN. For Bo Lind, who has no orders, the join pads o.total_cents with NULL, and the predicate NULL > 5000 is not true - it is UNKNOWN - so the row is filtered out. The first query returns 2 rows and Bo is gone. Moving the condition into the ON clause changes its job: it now decides which orders are eligible to match, not which output rows survive, and the second query returns 3 rows with Bo present on a NULL-padded row. The rule: conditions on the optional (right) side of a LEFT JOIN belong in ON if they are about matching, and in WHERE only if you genuinely want to discard the unmatched rows too. Conditions on the preserved (left) side are safe in WHERE, because those columns are never NULL-padded. When a LEFT JOIN 'stops working' after an edit, a WHERE predicate on the right table is the first suspect, every time.
Revenue per order looks inflated ever since I joined order_lines into the query. The order totals are being counted multiple times - show me the bug and the fix.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE order_lines (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id), qty INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (201, 10000), (202, 5000)
SELECT SUM(o.total_cents) AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN order_lines l ON l.order_id = o.id
SELECT SUM(total_cents) AS revenue FROM orders
SELECT SUM(o.total_cents) AS revenue FROM orders o JOIN (SELECT order_id, SUM(qty) AS units FROM order_lines GROUP BY order_id) u ON u.order_id = o.id

messages.content: The join fans out: order 201 has 3 lines, so its row is duplicated 3 times in the joined stream, and SUM sees its 10000 cents three times. The buggy total is 35000 cents against a true revenue of 15000 cents - inflated by exactly the extra copies. The third query shows the structural fix when you really need line data alongside order data: pre-aggregate the many side down to one row per order inside a subquery, then join. One row in, one row out, and the total comes back to 15000. Diagnose fan-out by asking, for every join, 'can one row on the left match several on the right?' If yes, any aggregate over a column from the one side is suspect. COUNT has the same disease - COUNT(o.id) would count lines, not orders - and the bandage COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) fixes counts but does nothing for SUM. Pre-aggregation is the cure because it removes the duplication instead of compensating for it.
Students take many courses and courses have many students. How do I list which courses each student is enrolled in, and count enrollments per course?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE students (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE courses (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES students(id), course_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES courses(id), PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id))
INSERT INTO students VALUES (1, 'Mina'), (2, 'Owen'), (3, 'Priya')
INSERT INTO courses VALUES (10, 'Algebra'), (20, 'Biology'), (30, 'Ceramics')
INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (1, 10), (1, 20), (2, 10), (3, 10), (3, 30)
SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id ORDER BY s.name, c.title

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	title
Mina	Algebra
Mina	Biology
Owen	Algebra
Priya	Algebra
Priya	Ceramics

arguments.sql: SELECT c.title, COUNT(*) AS enrolled FROM courses c JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title ORDER BY enrolled DESC, c.title

messages.content: A many-to-many relationship cannot live in either table - a student row cannot hold a list of courses - so it gets its own bridge table, enrollments, whose composite primary key (student_id, course_id) also prevents double-enrollment. Answering 'who takes what' is then two ordinary joins chained through the bridge, yielding 5 enrollment rows. Counting per course groups the bridge itself: Algebra leads with 3 students, and note that Biology and Ceramics tie at the bottom of this small roster. Two things worth internalizing: the bridge table is where relationship attributes belong (enrollment date, grade, status) because they describe the pairing, not either side; and every many-to-many query you will ever write is this same shape - entity, bridge, entity - with the joins pointing at the bridge's foreign keys. If you find yourself joining students directly to courses on a shared column, the schema, not the query, is what needs fixing.
Commissions are paid by deal size: under $100 earns 5%, $100 to $999 earns 8%, $1000 and up earns 12%. The bands live in a table. How do I attach the right rate to each sale?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE bands (label TEXT NOT NULL, min_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, max_cents INTEGER, rate REAL NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE sales (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, rep TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO bands VALUES ('small', 0, 9999, 0.05), ('mid', 10000, 99999, 0.08), ('large', 100000, NULL, 0.12)

SELECT s.id, s.rep, s.amount_cents, b.label, CAST(ROUND(s.amount_cents * b.rate) AS INTEGER) AS commission_cents FROM sales s JOIN bands b ON s.amount_cents >= b.min_cents AND (b.max_cents IS NULL OR s.amount_cents <= b.max_cents) ORDER BY s.id

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
id	rep	amount_cents	label	commission_cents
1	Ana	5000	small	250
2	Ana	25000	mid	2000
3	Bo	150000	large	18000
4	Bo	9999	small	500
5	Cy	100000	large	12000

Not every join key is an equality. This is a range join: each sale is matched to the band whose [min_cents, max_cents] interval contains its amount, and all 5 sales land in exactly one band - sale 4 at 9999 cents just makes 'small', while sale 5 at exactly 100000 cents falls into 'large' because the mid band's ceiling is 99999. The open-ended top band is modeled with a NULL max_cents plus the explicit IS NULL escape in the predicate; without that clause the largest deals would match nothing and silently drop out of an inner join. Range joins carry two design obligations equality joins do not. First, the bands must tile the number line with no gaps and no overlaps - a gap loses rows, an overlap duplicates them, and the database will not warn you about either. Second, boundary ownership has to be a decision, not an accident: here lower bounds are inclusive and upper bounds inclusive because the next band starts one cent higher. When you inherit a band table, verify the tiling with a quick check for overlaps before trusting any report built on it.
I joined shipments to warehouse scans on the city name to count scans per shipment, and the numbers exploded - way more rows than there are shipments. What went wrong?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE shipments (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, city TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE scans (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, city TEXT NOT NULL, kind TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO shipments VALUES (1, 'Austin'), (2, 'Austin'), (3, 'Denver')
INSERT INTO scans VALUES (11, 'Austin', 'arrive'), (12, 'Austin', 'sort'), (13, 'Austin', 'load'), (14, 'Denver', 'arrive')
SELECT COUNT(*) AS joined_rows FROM shipments s JOIN scans sc ON sc.city = s.city
SELECT s.id, COUNT(sc.id) AS scan_rows FROM shipments s JOIN scans sc ON sc.city = s.city GROUP BY s.id ORDER BY s.id

messages.content: City is not a key - it does not identify a shipment or a scan - so the join matched every Austin shipment against every Austin scan. With 2 Austin shipments and 3 Austin scans, that pairing alone produces 6 rows, and the full join returns 7 rows from only 3 shipments and 4 scans. Grouped per shipment the fiction is obvious: each Austin shipment is credited with 3 scans, as if every scan in the city belonged to it personally. When both sides of a join condition can repeat the value, the output size is the product of the duplicates, and aggregates over it are meaningless multiples. The fix is not a cleverer query; it is a real relationship: scans should carry the shipment_id they belong to, declared as a foreign key, and the join should run on that. A useful smoke test for any join you did not design: compare the joined row count against the larger input's row count. If a supposed one-to-many join returns more rows than the many side holds, something on the 'one' side is not unique, and every number downstream is inflated.
We migrated between two signup systems. I need one list showing which email addresses exist only in the old system, only in the new one, or in both.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE old_users (email TEXT PRIMARY KEY)
CREATE TABLE new_users (email TEXT PRIMARY KEY)
INSERT INTO old_users VALUES ('ana@x.com'), ('bo@x.com'), ('cy@x.com')
INSERT INTO new_users VALUES ('bo@x.com'), ('cy@x.com'), ('dee@x.com')

SELECT email, 'old only' AS presence FROM old_users WHERE email NOT IN (SELECT email FROM new_users) UNION ALL SELECT email, 'new only' FROM new_users WHERE email NOT IN (SELECT email FROM old_users) UNION ALL SELECT email, 'both' FROM old_users WHERE email IN (SELECT email FROM new_users) ORDER BY email

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
email	presence
ana@x.com	old only
bo@x.com	both
cy@x.com	both
dee@x.com	new only

That is a full outer comparison, and the portable way to build one is to assemble it from three honest pieces, as done here: anti-join in one direction, anti-join in the other, and the intersection. The combined result has 4 rows - ana@x.com is old only, dee@x.com is new only, and the two shared addresses report 'both'. Each piece uses NOT IN / IN against the other table's key, which is safe here because email is a primary key and therefore never NULL; with a nullable column, NOT IN would need replacing by NOT EXISTS, a trap covered elsewhere in this corpus. Newer SQLite versions do offer FULL OUTER JOIN directly, and it would produce the matched/unmatched row pairs in one statement - but it hands you NULL-padded rows you still have to classify with CASE, and it hides which of the three buckets a row came from. The UNION ALL assembly is longer yet each branch states its meaning, the ORDER BY applies to the whole union, and the pattern ports to every database you will ever touch. For reconciliation work, explicit and portable beats terse.
I need a report of daily sales for each store for a week, and days with no sales must still appear as zero rather than being absent. How do I force the missing days into existence?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE stores (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE sales (store_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES stores(id), sale_date TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO stores VALUES (1, 'North'), (2, 'South')

WITH days(d) AS (SELECT '2026-11-02' UNION ALL SELECT '2026-11-03' UNION ALL SELECT '2026-11-04') SELECT st.name, d AS day, COALESCE(SUM(s.amount_cents), 0) AS day_total FROM stores st CROSS JOIN days d LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.store_id = st.id AND s.sale_date = d GROUP BY st.id, st.name, d ORDER BY st.name, d

messages.content: A table of sales can only contain days that had sales, so the missing days have to come from somewhere else: a scaffold. The CROSS JOIN of 2 stores against a 3-day calendar CTE produces the full 6-cell grid first, and the LEFT JOIN then fills each cell with that day's sales or NULL, which COALESCE renders as 0. 3 of the cells are zeros - days the raw sales table simply has no rows for, including South on 2026-11-02 and 2026-11-04. Notice the join condition carries both store and date, and the date condition sits in the ON clause, not WHERE - filtering in WHERE would delete the zero cells the scaffold exists to create. This scaffold pattern generalizes everywhere reporting meets time: months with no signups, categories with no returns, reps with no calls. Build the grid of what should exist, then let the facts attach to it. In production the day list usually comes from a recursive CTE calendar rather than hand-listed dates, but the shape of the query does not change.
Our CRM and billing system both have customer emails, but they disagree on capitalization and stray spaces, so a plain join on email matches almost nothing. How do I reconcile them?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE crm (email TEXT NOT NULL, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE billing (email TEXT NOT NULL, plan TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO crm VALUES ('Ana@X.com', 'Ana Ruiz'), (' bo@x.com ', 'Bo Lind'), ('CY@x.com', 'Cy Park'), ('dee@x.com', 'Dee Osei')
INSERT INTO billing VALUES ('ana@x.com', 'pro'), ('bo@x.com', 'free'), ('cy@x.com', 'pro'), ('eli@x.com', 'team')
SELECT COUNT(*) AS matched FROM crm c JOIN billing b ON b.email = c.email
SELECT c.name, b.plan FROM crm c JOIN billing b ON LOWER(TRIM(b.email)) = LOWER(TRIM(c.email)) ORDER BY c.name

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	plan
Ana Ruiz	pro
Bo Lind	free
Cy Park	pro

The plain equality join matches 0 of the 4 CRM rows - Bo's record is padded with spaces and the others differ by case, and string equality forgives none of that. Normalizing both sides inside the join condition with LOWER(TRIM(...)) matches 3 customers, leaving Dee (CRM only) and Eli (billing only) as the genuine discrepancies to investigate. Treat this as a diagnostic and a bridge, not a destination. A join on expressions cannot use an ordinary index on email, so it scans; fine for a reconciliation report, poor as a permanent integration. The durable fix is to clean the data once - normalize on write, store the canonical form, ideally with a UNIQUE constraint on the normalized column - and then join on the clean key. Until then, keep the two failure counts separate in your head: rows lost to formatting are a data-quality bug with a known cure, while rows missing on one side entirely are a business discrepancy. Conflating them makes the reconciliation look worse, and murkier, than it is.
I want to compare, for the same route on the same day, every pair of flights offered by different airlines, with the price difference. Same table on both sides - how?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE flights (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, route TEXT NOT NULL, flight_date TEXT NOT NULL, airline TEXT NOT NULL, price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)

SELECT a.airline AS pricier, b.airline AS cheaper, a.price_cents - b.price_cents AS diff_cents FROM flights a JOIN flights b ON a.route = b.route AND a.flight_date = b.flight_date AND a.airline <> b.airline AND a.price_cents > b.price_cents ORDER BY diff_cents DESC

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
pricier	cheaper	diff_cents
AirC	AirB	3800
AirC	AirA	2300
AirA	AirB	1500

A self-join treats one table as two independent copies - aliases a and b - and pairs rows with each other. The pairing conditions do the real work: same route and same date define the comparison set, airline <> airline forbids pairing a flight with itself or a same-airline twin, and price > price keeps each unordered pair exactly once, oriented from pricier to cheaper. The result is 3 pairs, all from the three-airline day: the widest gap is AirC over AirB by 3800 cents. Drop the price inequality and you get every pair twice, once in each direction, plus - without the airline condition - every flight paired with itself at a difference of zero. Those symmetric duplicates are the signature bug of self-joins, and the cure is always an ordering predicate on some column that breaks the tie between the two copies. Self-joins shine whenever the relationship lives inside one table: employee/manager, flight pairs, duplicate detection, sequential events. Reach for two aliases, then spend your care on the conditions that keep the pairing honest.
After joining orders to order_lines, my 'customers who ordered' count came out higher than the number of orders. Counting seems broken after joins.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE order_lines (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id), sku TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (301, 7), (302, 7), (303, 8)
SELECT COUNT(o.customer_id) AS naive_count, COUNT(*) AS joined_rows FROM orders o JOIN order_lines l ON l.order_id = o.id
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS distinct_customers, COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) AS distinct_orders FROM orders o JOIN order_lines l ON l.order_id = o.id

messages.content: Counting is not broken - it is honestly counting the joined stream, which has 6 rows because the join replicated each order once per line. COUNT(o.customer_id) therefore reports 6, counting customer 7 four times. COUNT(DISTINCT ...) collapses the copies first: 2 distinct customers and 3 distinct orders, which matches the orders table you started with. The discipline is to ask of every aggregate after a join: 'what is one row of the joined stream worth?' If the join fans out, row-level columns from the many side are fine to sum, but anything from the one side - counts, totals, averages - is being weighted by line count. COUNT(DISTINCT) is the right patch for counts. For sums of one-side columns there is no DISTINCT variant of SUM that saves you in standard SQL practice (SQLite does allow SUM(DISTINCT col), but it dedupes equal values, not duplicated rows - two orders of the same total would collapse wrongly). The structural fix is to aggregate each table at its own grain and join the results, so nothing is ever counted at the wrong grain.
A colleague writes FROM orders, customers WHERE customers.id = orders.customer_id instead of an explicit JOIN. Is that actually different, or just older style?

For an inner join the two forms are semantically identical - I ran both against the same fixture and each returned 3 rows, and any modern optimizer plans them the same way. The comma form is the pre-1992 syntax, and the join predicate lives in the WHERE clause mixed in with genuine filters. So why insist on explicit JOIN? Three practical reasons. First, safety: forget the predicate in the comma form and you silently get a Cartesian product - every order paired with every customer - while the JOIN form makes a missing ON clause a syntax error rather than a wrong answer. Second, expressiveness: LEFT JOIN, the tool you need the moment unmatched rows matter, has no comma equivalent at all, so the comma style caps what you can write. Third, readability under maintenance: in a five-table query, ON clauses keep each pairing next to its tables, while a WHERE clause holding four join predicates and three filters forces the reader to sort out which is which. Same results, same plan - but one style fails loudly and scales to outer joins, and the other fails silently. That is the whole argument.
Our biggest report joins orders, customers, and shipments. It is slow and I cannot tell which stage shrinks the data. Walk me through staging the join so I can see the row counts at each step.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, region TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id), status TEXT NOT NULL, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE shipments (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id), carrier TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'SE'), (2, 'SE'), (3, 'NW'), (4, 'SE')

INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 1, 'shipped', 5000), (2, 1, 'pending', 3000), (3, 2, 'shipped', 7000), (4, 3, 'shipped', 9000), (5, 4, 'cancelled', 2000), (6, 4, 'shipped', 4500), (7, 2, 'shipped', 6200), (8, 3, 'pending', 1500)
INSERT INTO shipments VALUES (21, 1, 'UPS'), (22, 3, 'FedEx'), (23, 4, 'UPS'), (24, 6, 'DHL'), (25, 7, 'UPS')
SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_orders FROM orders
SELECT COUNT(*) AS shipped_orders FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped'
SELECT COUNT(*) AS se_shipped FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'shipped' AND c.region = 'SE'
SELECT COUNT(*) AS with_shipment_row FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id JOIN shipments s ON s.order_id = o.id WHERE o.status = 'shipped' AND c.region = 'SE'

messages.content: Staging turns one opaque query into a funnel you can read: 8 orders total, 5 after the status filter, 4 after joining customers and keeping the SE region (the NW shipped order falls away at this stage), and 4 once shipments are joined - in this data the shipment join loses nothing, because every SE shipped order already has its shipment row; had one been missing, this is exactly the stage where the funnel would have exposed it, where the monolithic query would have hidden it inside a single wrong total. The method matters more than these particular numbers. Apply one transformation at a time and count after each: filters first, then joins in the order the report builds them. The stage where the count moves unexpectedly is where your bug or your cost lives - a filter that kills 90% of rows should run before any join, and a join that multiplies rows announces a fan-out before it poisons an aggregate. Once the funnel is understood, fold the stages back into a single statement with the selective predicates pushed as early as the semantics allow. Optimizers are good, but they cannot fix a join that should have been a LEFT JOIN, and they cannot tell you that a missing shipment row, not slowness, was the real story.
Just show me plainly: which member borrowed which book, sorted by member name?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE members (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE loans (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, member_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES members(id), book_title TEXT NOT NULL, borrowed_on TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO members VALUES (1, 'Ana Ruiz'), (2, 'Bo Lind'), (3, 'Cy Park')
SELECT m.name, l.book_title, l.borrowed_on FROM loans l JOIN members m ON m.id = l.member_id ORDER BY m.name, l.borrowed_on

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	book_title	borrowed_on
Ana Ruiz	Emma	2026-11-03
Ana Ruiz	Dune	2026-11-10
Bo Lind	Dune	2026-11-01
Cy Park	Hamlet	2026-11-08

The loans table stores member_id, a foreign key - a number, not a name - so the JOIN translates it back into the member's name for every loan. All 4 loans appear, Ana Ruiz twice (Emma on 2026-11-03 and Dune on 2026-11-10), because the join produces one row per loan, not per member. That one-row-per-what question is the first thing to settle in any join: the grain of the output is the grain of the driving table, here loans. If you wanted one row per member with their books strung together, that is a different query (GROUP_CONCAT territory), not a tweak of this one. Note also the direction of reading: FROM loans JOIN members works because each loan has exactly one member. Starting FROM members with the same inner join would return the identical four rows - inner joins do not care which side you list first - but the mental model 'for each loan, find its member' matches the foreign key's direction and keeps the next person from wondering where orderless members went. They were never in scope: this question was about loans.
Revenue by sales rep, but two reps closed nothing this quarter and the report must show them with 0, not omit them or show blank.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE reps (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE deals (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, rep_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES reps(id), amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO reps VALUES (1, 'Ana'), (2, 'Bo'), (3, 'Cy'), (4, 'Dee')
SELECT r.name, SUM(d.amount_cents) AS revenue FROM reps r LEFT JOIN deals d ON d.rep_id = r.id GROUP BY r.id, r.name ORDER BY r.name

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	revenue
Ana	20000
Bo	NULL
Cy	15000
Dee	NULL

arguments.sql: SELECT r.name, COALESCE(SUM(d.amount_cents), 0) AS revenue FROM reps r LEFT JOIN deals d ON d.rep_id = r.id GROUP BY r.id, r.name ORDER BY revenue DESC, r.name

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	revenue
Ana	20000
Cy	15000
Bo	0
Dee	0

The LEFT JOIN keeps all 4 reps, but look at the raw version: for Bo and Dee the SUM is NULL, not 0, because SUM over a set of NULL-padded rows has nothing to add - an aggregate over zero real values returns NULL in SQL. COALESCE converts that NULL into the 0 the report needs, and the final ranking puts Ana's 20000 cents and Cy's 15000 ahead of the two zeros. Bo and Dee show 0, present and accounted for, which is what 'the report must show them' actually requires: a row, with a number, not an absence a reader might mistake for a rendering bug. Keep the two ideas separate in your toolbox: LEFT JOIN decides which rows exist; COALESCE decides what empty values print as. And be deliberate about which one a stakeholder means - a rep with no deals (0) is a different statement from a rep whose figures are unknown (NULL). Reports usually want the former; audits sometimes need the latter preserved.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE users (tenant_id INTEGER NOT NULL, id INTEGER NOT NULL, name TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, id))
CREATE TABLE sessions (tenant_id INTEGER NOT NULL, user_id INTEGER NOT NULL, token TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 1, 'TenantA Ana'), (2, 1, 'TenantB Bo'), (1, 2, 'TenantA Cy')
INSERT INTO sessions VALUES (1, 1, 'tok-a1'), (2, 1, 'tok-b1'), (1, 2, 'tok-a2')
SELECT s.token, u.name FROM sessions s JOIN users u ON u.id = s.user_id ORDER BY s.token

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
token	name
tok-a1	TenantA Ana
tok-a1	TenantB Bo
tok-a2	TenantA Cy
tok-b1	TenantA Ana
tok-b1	TenantB Bo

arguments.sql: SELECT s.token, u.name FROM sessions s JOIN users u ON u.id = s.user_id AND u.tenant_id = s.tenant_id ORDER BY s.token

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
token	name
tok-a1	TenantA Ana
tok-a2	TenantA Cy
tok-b1	TenantB Bo

Joining on id alone produced 5 rows from 3 sessions: user id 1 exists in both tenants, so each session with user_id 1 matched both Ana of tenant 1 and Bo of tenant 2 - tok-a1 was attributed to a person in a different company. That is not a cosmetic bug; in a multi-tenant system it is a data-leak class bug. The correct join carries the full composite key - id AND tenant_id - and returns exactly 3 rows, each session with its own tenant's user. The principle generalizes: a join must equate the entire key of the referenced table, whatever that key is. When a primary key is composite (tenant_id, id), a partial-key join is not a shortcut, it is a different, wrong relationship that happens to type-check. Defenses stack up well here: declare the foreign key as the composite pair so the database enforces it, keep tenant_id on every tenant-owned table even when it feels redundant, and treat any join in this codebase that mentions id without tenant_id as a review blocker. The database cannot know tenants must never mix; the schema and the join conditions are where that rule lives.
Give me the staff directory as a table: each employee, their department, and their manager's name.

| Employee | Department | Manager |
|---|---|---|
| Ana | Kitchen | Marla |
| Bo | Kitchen | Ana |
| Cy | Floor | Marla |
| Dee | Floor | Cy |
| Marla | Office | (none) |

Two different joins do two different jobs in one query: the inner join to departments is safe because every employee must belong to one, while the manager join must be a LEFT JOIN against the employees table itself - a self-join - because the top of the chart, Marla, has manager_id NULL and an inner join would silently fire her from her own directory. COALESCE renders her missing manager as '(none)' rather than a blank that looks like missing data. Someone on my team used NATURAL JOIN for a report and rows quietly disappeared compared to the old explicit join. Same tables, fewer rows. Explain and demonstrate.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE tickets (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, status TEXT NOT NULL, agent_id INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE agents (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO agents VALUES (7, 'Ana', 'active'), (8, 'Bo', 'on leave')
INSERT INTO tickets VALUES (1, 'open', 7), (2, 'closed', 7), (3, 'open', 8)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS natural_rows FROM tickets t NATURAL JOIN agents a
SELECT COUNT(*) AS explicit_rows FROM tickets t JOIN agents a ON a.id = t.agent_id

messages.content: NATURAL JOIN does not join on the key you mean - it joins on every column the two tables happen to share a name for, all of them, with equality. These tables share two names: id and status. The natural version therefore demands t.id = a.id AND t.status = a.status, a relationship nobody intended, and it returns 0 rows. The explicit join on agent_id returns 3, one per ticket. The deeper danger is temporal: NATURAL JOIN's meaning changes when the schema changes. Add a status column to tickets next quarter for an unrelated feature and every natural join against agents silently tightens its matching and starts dropping rows, with no change to the query text and no error anywhere. Code review cannot see it, because the query looks identical. USING (agent_id) is the middle option - it names the shared column explicitly and even merges it in the output - but the professional default is ON with fully qualified columns: verbose once, stable forever. If you inherit NATURAL JOINs, treat converting them as preventive maintenance, not style pedantry: each one is a schema change away from a silent data loss.
How many products do we stock in each category? One row per category with a count.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, category TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO products VALUES (1, 'Notebook', 'paper'), (2, 'Pen', 'paper'), (3, 'Mug', 'kitchen'), (4, 'Kettle', 'kitchen'), (5, 'Plate', 'kitchen'), (6, 'Lamp', 'lighting')
SELECT category, COUNT(*) AS products FROM products GROUP BY category ORDER BY products DESC, category
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM products

messages.content: GROUP BY partitions the table into one bucket per distinct category and COUNT(*) tallies each bucket: kitchen leads with 3, then paper with 2 and lighting with 1. The buckets sum to 6, the full table - grouping never creates or destroys rows, it only sorts them into piles and reports per pile. Two details worth fixing in memory. The ORDER BY here sorts by the aggregate (products DESC), which is allowed because ordering happens after grouping; without it, group order is unspecified even if it looks stable on small data. And COUNT(*) counts rows in the group, whatever they contain - the right choice for 'how many products', distinct from COUNT of a specific column, which skips NULLs and answers a subtly different question. Every GROUP BY query is this same skeleton: choose the grouping column (the grain of the answer), choose the aggregate (the fact per grain), and check the grains add back up to the whole.
Total paid hours per department for the week, from the shifts table.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE shifts (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, dept TEXT NOT NULL, hours REAL NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO shifts VALUES (1, 'Kitchen', 7.5), (2, 'Kitchen', 6.0), (3, 'Floor', 8.0), (4, 'Floor', 5.5), (5, 'Floor', 4.0), (6, 'Office', 7.0)
SELECT dept, SUM(hours) AS total_hours, COUNT(*) AS shifts FROM shifts GROUP BY dept ORDER BY total_hours DESC

messages.name: database_query

dept	total_hours	shifts
Floor	17.5	3
Kitchen	13.5	2
Office	7.0	1

SUM collapses each department's shifts into one total: Floor 17.5 hours across 3 shifts, Kitchen 13.5 across 2, and Office 7.0 from its single shift. Carrying COUNT(*) alongside the sum is a cheap sanity habit - it tells the reader how much data each total rests on, and a department whose hours look wrong with only one shift is a different investigation from one with thirty. Note the hours are REAL values and these particular ones (halves and wholes) sum exactly in floating point; money and hours in production schemas are safer as integers - cents and minutes - because long sums of binary floats drift by fractions that reconciliation then has to explain.
