I need departments whose total sales exceed $1,000. I tried putting SUM(amount) > 100000 in the WHERE clause and got an error. Where does that condition belong?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE sales (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, dept TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1, 'Kitchen', 40000), (2, 'Kitchen', 45000), (3, 'Kitchen', 30000), (4, 'Floor', 25000), (5, 'Floor', 20000), (6, 'Office', 90000)
SELECT dept, SUM(amount_cents) AS total FROM sales GROUP BY dept HAVING SUM(amount_cents) > 100000 ORDER BY total DESC
SELECT dept, SUM(amount_cents) AS total FROM sales WHERE amount_cents > 30000 GROUP BY dept ORDER BY total DESC

messages.content: Conditions on aggregates belong in HAVING, which runs after grouping; conditions on raw rows belong in WHERE, which runs before. Your error was a phase mistake: WHERE is evaluated row by row, at a moment when SUM does not exist yet. With HAVING, only Kitchen qualifies, at 115000 cents. The second query shows the two phases cooperating - and how much damage a misplaced condition does: WHERE first discards every individual sale of 30000 cents or less, and the picture changes completely. Office now leads at 90000 cents, Kitchen's total shrinks because one of its sales never reached the grouping stage, and Floor vanishes altogether - not because its total was small, but because no single Floor sale cleared a bar that was supposed to apply to totals. The mental model is an assembly line: FROM assembles rows, WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY piles them, HAVING filters piles, SELECT shapes output, ORDER BY sorts. Most 'why is my aggregate query wrong' bugs are a condition standing at the wrong station on that line. When a filter mentions an aggregate function it belongs in HAVING; when it mentions only stored columns it usually belongs in WHERE - and moving a condition from HAVING to WHERE is an optimization only when it does not change which rows get grouped.
When I group orders by coupon_code, one of the groups has a blank coupon. There is no empty-string coupon in the data. Where did that group come from?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, coupon_code TEXT, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'SAVE10', 5000), (2, NULL, 3000), (3, 'SAVE10', 2000), (4, NULL, 4500), (5, 'FREESHIP', 6000), (6, NULL, 1500)
SELECT coupon_code, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(total_cents) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY coupon_code ORDER BY revenue DESC

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
coupon_code	orders	revenue
NULL	3	9000
SAVE10	2	7000
FREESHIP	1	6000

The blank group is the NULL group: 3 orders were placed without any coupon, and GROUP BY collects all NULLs into a single group of their own - here worth 9000 cents, the largest revenue bucket of the three. The blank is not an empty string and not a rendering glitch; the coupon column is genuinely NULL for those rows, meaning 'no coupon', and the group label prints as nothing. This behavior is a quiet exception to NULL's usual refusal to compare equal: for grouping (and for DISTINCT and UNION), SQL treats NULLs as peers so they can be bucketed together, even though NULL = NULL in a WHERE clause is UNKNOWN, not true. For reports, label the group deliberately - COALESCE(coupon_code, '(none)') in the SELECT makes the bucket self-describing and stops a stakeholder from reading the blank as missing data. And when a grouped report's totals exceed the sum of the visible labeled groups, a hidden NULL group is the usual explanation: always reconcile grouped output against the ungrouped total.
For each class I need the name of the highest-scoring student. I wrote SELECT class, name, MAX(score) FROM results GROUP BY class and it gave me names - can I trust them?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE results (class TEXT NOT NULL, name TEXT NOT NULL, score INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO results VALUES ('A', 'Mina', 88), ('A', 'Owen', 95), ('A', 'Priya', 95), ('B', 'Sam', 72), ('B', 'Tess', 81)
SELECT class, name, MAX(score) AS top_score FROM results GROUP BY class ORDER BY class

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
class	name	top_score
A	Owen	95
B	Tess	81

arguments.sql: SELECT r.class, r.name, r.score FROM results r WHERE r.score = (SELECT MAX(score) FROM results WHERE class = r.class) ORDER BY r.class, r.name

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
class	name	score
A	Owen	95
A	Priya	95
B	Tess	81

In SQLite, mostly - with one sharp caveat. SQLite has a documented special behavior: when a query uses exactly one MIN or MAX aggregate, bare columns like name are taken from a row that achieved the maximum, so here it reports Owen for class A at 95 and Tess for class B. But class A has a tie - both Owen and Priya scored 95 - and the bare-column form silently shows just one of them, chosen by scan order. The correlated form, which asks for every row equal to its class maximum, returns 3 rows and exposes the tie honestly. Portability makes the case stronger: in PostgreSQL, MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY, and standard SQL generally, selecting a bare non-grouped column beside an aggregate is an error or undefined behavior, precisely because the database refuses to guess which row's name you meant. The SQLite shortcut is safe only when ties are impossible or irrelevant. When the question is 'who achieved the extreme', write the query that returns all achievers and decide what ties mean as a business rule, not as an accident of row order.
COUNT(*), COUNT(email), and COUNT(DISTINCT email) give me three different numbers on the same survey table. Which counts what?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE survey (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT)
INSERT INTO survey VALUES (1, 'ana@x.com'), (2, 'bo@x.com'), (3, NULL), (4, 'ana@x.com'), (5, NULL), (6, 'cy@x.com'), (7, 'bo@x.com')
SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows, COUNT(email) AS with_email, COUNT(DISTINCT email) AS distinct_emails FROM survey

messages.content: Three questions, three answers, all correct: COUNT(*) = 7 counts rows, full stop - it never looks at any column. COUNT(email) = 5 counts rows where email is not NULL, because column-counts skip NULLs by design. COUNT(DISTINCT email) = 3 counts the distinct non-NULL addresses - ana and bo each answered twice, cy once. Each number answers a different stakeholder question: rows received (7), responses with a usable contact (5), and unique respondents (3). Reports go wrong when the writer picks the count whose name sounds closest rather than the one matching the question - 'how many people responded' is the DISTINCT figure, while 'how many responses' is the row count, and using COUNT(email) for either quietly writes the two NULL rows out of history. One more wrinkle: COUNT(DISTINCT email) is case-sensitive in SQLite, so 'Ana@x.com' and 'ana@x.com' would count as two people. If identity matters, count a normalized form - COUNT(DISTINCT LOWER(TRIM(email))) - and say so in the report, because deduplication rules are part of the number's meaning.
I need signups per month split by channel - web and mobile as separate columns, not separate rows.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE signups (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, channel TEXT NOT NULL, signed_on TEXT NOT NULL)

SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', signed_on) AS month, SUM(CASE WHEN channel = 'web' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS web, SUM(CASE WHEN channel = 'mobile' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS mobile, COUNT(*) AS total FROM signups GROUP BY month ORDER BY month

messages.content: This is conditional aggregation - a pivot built from ordinary aggregates. Each row of the group contributes 1 to exactly one channel column: the CASE turns a matching row into 1 and everything else into 0, and SUM adds the flags. The result reads across: 2026-09 web 2 / mobile 1, 2026-10 web 1 / mobile 3, 2026-11 web 1 / mobile 0, and the COUNT(*) column reconciles each row (3, 4, 1). SQLite also offers COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE channel = 'web'), which is the same idea with cleaner syntax where supported; the CASE form works everywhere and makes the logic visible. Two habits keep pivots honest: always include the unconditioned total so readers can verify the columns add up, and decide in advance what a channel value you did not anticipate (say 'partner') should do - with this shape it lands in the total but in no column, which the reconciliation column exposes immediately instead of letting the discrepancy hide.
Sales by city, but the report also needs a subtotal per region and a grand total at the bottom - all from one query.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE sales (region TEXT NOT NULL, city TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO sales VALUES ('SE', 'Orlando', 5000), ('SE', 'Orlando', 3000), ('SE', 'Miami', 7000), ('NW', 'Seattle', 9000), ('NW', 'Portland', 4000)

SELECT region, city, SUM(amount_cents) AS total, 0 AS level FROM sales GROUP BY region, city UNION ALL SELECT region, 'ALL CITIES', SUM(amount_cents), 1 FROM sales GROUP BY region UNION ALL SELECT 'ALL REGIONS', 'ALL CITIES', SUM(amount_cents), 2 FROM sales ORDER BY region, level, city

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
region	city	total	level
ALL REGIONS	ALL CITIES	28000	2
NW	Portland	4000	0
NW	Seattle	9000	0
NW	ALL CITIES	13000	1
SE	Miami	7000	0
SE	Orlando	8000	0
SE	ALL CITIES	15000	1

SQLite has no ROLLUP operator, so you build one from its parts: the same aggregation run at three grains - city, region, and everything - stacked with UNION ALL, with a level column recording which grain each row belongs to. The stack has 7 rows and the grand total lands at 28000 cents, which you can verify against the region subtotals by hand. The level column is not decoration: sorting needs it (subtotals must follow their cities, and text sorting alone would scatter 'ALL CITIES' among real city names), and consumers of the result need it to style or filter grains without parsing labels. Keep the sentinel labels ('ALL CITIES', 'ALL REGIONS') in the data columns rather than NULL, because a NULL city in this output would be indistinguishable from a genuine data problem. And note the cost model: the table is scanned once per UNION ALL branch - three passes here. For a report that is fine; for a dashboard refreshed every minute, pre-aggregating into a summary table is the grown-up version of the same idea.
Average order value per customer segment is off - customers with big multi-line orders seem to count extra. I joined lines in to get the segment. What is the correct shape?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, segment TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id), total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE order_lines (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id), qty INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'retail'), (2, 'retail'), (3, 'trade')
SELECT c.segment, AVG(o.total_cents) AS aov FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id JOIN order_lines l ON l.order_id = o.id GROUP BY c.segment ORDER BY c.segment
SELECT c.segment, AVG(o.total_cents) AS aov FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.segment ORDER BY c.segment

messages.content: The joined version computes retail AOV as 9200.0 cents; the true figure is 8000.0. The join replicated order 11 once per line - 4 copies - so the average became a weighted average where the weight is line count, and the biggest, most complex order dragged the segment's AOV down toward itself four times over. Trade is the exception that proves the mechanism: it has a single order, so replicating that order's rows cannot move its average - 20000.0 cents either way - because fan-out distorts only when replicated rows mix at different weights inside one group. AVG is the aggregate most vulnerable to fan-out because the corruption is silent and plausible-looking; SUM at least has the decency to look inflated. The correct shape respects grains: average order value is a fact about orders, so its query touches customers and orders only. If the report genuinely needs line-level facts beside it (units per segment, say), aggregate each fact at its own grain in its own subquery and join the two summaries - never drag the detail table into the average's FROM clause 'just to have it available'. Grain discipline is the whole game: one query, one grain, or summaries joined after the fact.
Our average product rating shows 4.0, but support insists unhappy customers who skip the rating should drag it down. Who is right about what AVG does with missing ratings?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE reviews (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product TEXT NOT NULL, rating INTEGER)
INSERT INTO reviews VALUES (1, 'Kettle', 5), (2, 'Kettle', 4), (3, 'Kettle', NULL), (4, 'Kettle', 4), (5, 'Kettle', NULL), (6, 'Kettle', 3)
SELECT AVG(rating) AS avg_rating, COUNT(rating) AS rated, COUNT(*) AS total_reviews FROM reviews
SELECT AVG(COALESCE(rating, 0)) AS avg_if_zero FROM reviews

messages.content: AVG ignores NULLs entirely - it sums the non-NULL ratings and divides by how many there are. Here that is 16 points over 4 rated reviews = 4.0, and the 2 unrated reviews might as well not exist. If unrated counted as zero, the average would be 2.6666666666666665 - a very different story about the same product. Neither is 'the truth'; they answer different questions. AVG(rating) says 'among customers who rated, how did they rate' - the standard meaning of a displayed star average. AVG(COALESCE(rating,0)) says 'rate the response rate as dissatisfaction', which punishes products for review-form abandonment, shipping delays in the survey email, and every other reason a rating goes missing that has nothing to do with quality. The professional move is to report the pair together - average and coverage (rated out of total) - and let the reader judge. A 4.0 on 4 of 6 reviews is weaker evidence than a 4.0 on 400 of 410, and no single number can carry both facts. What you must not do is silently switch definitions between reports, because the trend line will jump and nobody will know the ruler changed.
For a catalog page I need each product's tags as one comma-separated string, not one row per tag.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE product_tags (product_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id), tag TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO products VALUES (1, 'Trail Shoes'), (2, 'Rain Jacket'), (3, 'Wool Socks')
INSERT INTO product_tags VALUES (1, 'waterproof'), (1, 'sale'), (1, 'new'), (2, 'waterproof'), (2, 'sale')
SELECT p.name, GROUP_CONCAT(t.tag, ', ') AS tags FROM products p LEFT JOIN product_tags t ON t.product_id = p.id GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY p.name

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	tags
Rain Jacket	sale, waterproof
Trail Shoes	new, sale, waterproof
Wool Socks	NULL

GROUP_CONCAT is the aggregate that builds lists: it folds each group's values into one string. Trail Shoes comes out as 'new, sale, waterproof' and Rain Jacket as 'sale, waterproof'. Wool Socks, having no tags, shows NULL through the LEFT JOIN - decide whether the page wants that rendered as an empty string via COALESCE, because a NULL in a JSON payload and an empty list are different statements. Now the warnings, which are the real lesson. The order of tags inside the string is not guaranteed by the aggregate itself; SQLite happens to follow scan order, and wrapping the input in an ordered subquery is the common way to coax a stable order, but no standard promises it. Second, GROUP_CONCAT destroys structure: once tags are a string, filtering 'products tagged sale' must go back to the table, not parse the string - this output is for display only. Third, the separator can collide with the data (a tag containing a comma), which is why display-only is a hard rule. Used as a presentation convenience at the end of a query whose filtering happened on real rows, it is exactly the right tool.
SQLite has no MEDIAN function. I need the median API response time from a metrics table - how do I get the middle value honestly?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE metrics (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, ms INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM metrics
SELECT AVG(ms) AS median_ms FROM (SELECT ms FROM metrics ORDER BY ms LIMIT 2 - (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM metrics) % 2 OFFSET ((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM metrics) - 1) / 2)
SELECT AVG(ms) AS mean_ms FROM metrics

messages.content: The median is a positional statistic, so you build it from ordering: sort the 7 values and average the middle one (odd count) or middle two (even count). The subquery encodes both cases in one expression - LIMIT 2 - (n % 2) takes 1 row for odd n and 2 for even, starting at OFFSET (n-1)/2 - and AVG over that tiny set yields the median, 180.0 ms here. Compare the mean, 193.57142857142858 ms: the single 340 ms outlier pulls it noticeably above the median, which is exactly why latency reporting prefers medians and percentiles - the typical request is better described by the middle than by an average taxed by the worst day. Handle the edges deliberately: an even count must average two values (taking just the lower one is a 'low median', a different statistic - fine if labeled, dishonest if not), and an empty table must return NULL rather than an error, which this shape does naturally since AVG of no rows is NULL. In larger systems you would reach for percentile functions or approximate sketches; in SQLite this ordered-window extraction is the honest exact method, and its cost is one sort of the column.
Quick check I can run myself: does the sum of my per-category totals actually equal the overall total? I want a query that proves the report adds up.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE sales (category TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO sales VALUES ('paper', 1200), ('paper', 800), ('kitchen', 2500), ('kitchen', 1500), ('lighting', 4000)
SELECT category, SUM(amount_cents) AS cat_total FROM sales GROUP BY category ORDER BY category
SELECT (SELECT SUM(amount_cents) FROM sales) AS overall, SUM(cat_total) AS sum_of_groups FROM (SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS cat_total FROM sales GROUP BY category)

messages.content: It does: the overall total is 10000 cents and the sum of the 3 category totals is also 10000. The check query computes the same quantity two independent ways - directly over the raw rows, and by re-aggregating the grouped result - and reconciliation is just comparing them. This two-ways habit catches the failures that eyeballing never does: a NULL category quietly forming a hidden group, a join upstream fanning rows out so the grouped report overstates the raw table, or a WHERE clause that exists in one version of the report and not the other. Whenever the two numbers disagree, the grouped pipeline - not the raw total - is where you dig, because the raw SUM over the base table has nowhere to hide. One asymmetry to respect: this check proves arithmetic consistency, not correctness of the categories themselves. If a sale was filed under the wrong category, both computations agree beautifully on the wrong split. Reconciliation validates the query; only source-data audits validate the data.
Find products that sold more than 8 units in total but whose average unit price is under $20 - a filter on two different aggregates at once.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE order_lines (product TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, unit_price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO order_lines VALUES ('Notebook', 5, 1200), ('Notebook', 4, 1100), ('Pen', 20, 300), ('Pen', 15, 350), ('Desk Lamp', 3, 4500), ('Desk Lamp', 2, 4700), ('Mug', 9, 2100), ('Mug', 1, 1900)
SELECT product, SUM(qty) AS units, AVG(unit_price_cents) AS avg_price FROM order_lines GROUP BY product HAVING SUM(qty) > 8 AND AVG(unit_price_cents) < 2000 ORDER BY units DESC

messages.content: HAVING accepts any combination of aggregate conditions, including conditions on aggregates that are not even in the SELECT list. Grouping first and then testing both thresholds leaves 2 products: Pen with 35 units at an average of 325.0 cents, and Notebook with 9 units at 1150.0 cents. The near-misses are instructive. Mug sold 10 units and its two lines average exactly 2000 cents - the mean of its 2100-cent and 1900-cent lines - so it fails the strictly-under-2000 test on the boundary; note the average is over lines, not weighted by quantity, so a 1-unit expensive line counts as much as a 9-unit cheap one; if the business means revenue-weighted price, the honest expression is SUM(qty*unit_price_cents)/SUM(qty), a different number answering a different question. Desk Lamp fails on units despite its price being nowhere near the threshold either way. State which average you mean whenever a filter involves one - line-average and unit-average diverge exactly when quantities vary, which is always.
Count signups per month from a table that stores full dates, so I can see growth month over month.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE signups (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, signed_on TEXT NOT NULL)
SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', signed_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS signups FROM signups GROUP BY month ORDER BY month

messages.content: Bucketing a date means mapping many dates onto one label and grouping by the label. strftime('%Y-%m', signed_on) truncates each ISO date to its year-month, and the counts come out 2026-08: 2, 2026-09: 3, 2026-10: 4 - a clean growth line. Two properties make this the right idiom. The '%Y-%m' label sorts chronologically as plain text, because ISO formats are lexicographically ordered - '2026-09' < '2026-10' works, while a '%m/%Y' label would sort October before September and wreck the chart. And grouping by the truncated label is exactly equivalent to grouping by date(signed_on, 'start of month'), just with a display-ready key. The trap waiting in month buckets is absence: a month with zero signups produces no group and vanishes from the trend, making a collapse look like a gap in the chart's axis. If the series must be continuous, scaffold the months with a calendar CTE and LEFT JOIN the counts onto it - the same grid pattern used for daily store sales elsewhere in this batch's family of techniques.
Our week runs Monday to Sunday. Bucket ticket volume by week, labeled by the Monday of each week.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE tickets (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, opened_on TEXT NOT NULL)
SELECT date(opened_on, '-' || ((CAST(strftime('%w', opened_on) AS INTEGER) + 6) % 7) || ' days') AS week_monday, COUNT(*) AS tickets FROM tickets GROUP BY week_monday ORDER BY week_monday

messages.content: The label for a Monday-start week is 'the most recent Monday on or before this date', and the arithmetic is: strftime('%w') numbers days 0=Sunday..6=Saturday, so (dow + 6) % 7 converts that to 'days since Monday' (Monday itself becomes 0, Sunday becomes 6), and subtracting that many days lands on the week's Monday. The buckets come out 2026-11-02: 3 tickets, 2026-11-09: 2, 2026-11-16: 2. Check the boundary cases, because week logic lives and dies there: Sunday 2026-11-08 belongs to the week of Monday 11-02 (it is day 6 of that week, not the start of a new one), and Monday 11-09 opens its own bucket. Both behaviors fall out of the formula - verify them by hand whenever you write week math, because an off-by-one here misfiles every Sunday forever. Why not strftime('%W') or '%Y-%W' labels? Those give week numbers (with their own year-boundary quirks) rather than a date you can join, display, and reason about, and '%W' assumes Monday start but numbers the partial first week of the year as week 00. A Monday date as the bucket key is unambiguous across years and plays well with the calendar-scaffold pattern when some weeks have no tickets at all.
Show each day's sales alongside the running total up to that day.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE daily_sales (sale_date TEXT PRIMARY KEY, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT sale_date, amount_cents, SUM(amount_cents) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) AS running_total FROM daily_sales ORDER BY sale_date

messages.content: A window function computes an aggregate without collapsing rows: each day keeps its own row and gains a running_total column - 1200 after day one, 2000, 3500, 4100, ending at 6200, which reconciles with the week's total. The OVER (ORDER BY sale_date) clause defines the window as 'every row up to and including me in date order', which is the default frame for an ordered aggregate window. Contrast this with GROUP BY, which would have destroyed the daily detail to produce totals. Window functions answer 'for each row, what does its neighborhood look like' - running totals, ranks, prior-row values - while GROUP BY answers 'for each group, what is the summary'. Choosing between them is choosing whether the detail rows survive. One discipline note: the window's ORDER BY and the query's ORDER BY are independent. The window ordering defines correctness (what 'up to' means); the outer ordering only arranges the printout. Always specify both explicitly, and give the window a unique ordering key - with duplicate dates, 'up to me' is ambiguous among the tied rows unless the frame or the key says otherwise.
Rank students by exam score. Two students tied at the top - I need to see how ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK each treat the tie.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE exams (student TEXT NOT NULL, score INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO exams VALUES ('Mina', 95), ('Owen', 95), ('Priya', 88), ('Sam', 88), ('Tess', 72)
SELECT student, score, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rn, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rnk, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS drnk FROM exams ORDER BY score DESC, student

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
student	score	rn	rnk	drnk
Mina	95	1	1	1
Owen	95	2	1	1
Priya	88	3	3	2
Sam	88	4	3	2
Tess	72	5	5	3

Same ordering, three numbering philosophies. ROW_NUMBER ignores the tie and just counts positions: Mina 1, Owen 2 - the tie is broken by whatever secondary order the rows happen to be scanned in, so the assignment of 1 vs 2 to the tied pair is arbitrary unless you add a deterministic tiebreaker to the window's ORDER BY. RANK gives both leaders 1, then skips to 3 for the 88s - Olympic-style, leaving a gap where the shared place 'used up' a number. DENSE_RANK also shares 1 but continues at 2, no gaps. Pick by what the number means downstream. ROW_NUMBER when you need a unique key per row (pagination, top-1-per-group) and ties are either impossible or resolved by a stated tiebreaker. RANK when the number is a competitive standing and a shared first place genuinely means nobody is second. DENSE_RANK when the number feeds a category like 'top 3 score levels' and gaps would break the counting. The silent bug to avoid is using ROW_NUMBER for a leaderboard: it manufactures a unique winner out of a tie, and the 'winner' can change between runs if the scan order changes. If the business has no tiebreak rule, the honest display is RANK.
For each day, show signups and how much they changed versus the previous day.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE daily_signups (day TEXT PRIMARY KEY, signups INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT day, signups, signups - LAG(signups) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS change_vs_prev FROM daily_signups ORDER BY day

messages.content: LAG reaches one row back inside the window and hands you the previous day's value, so the change is a plain subtraction per row: 2026-11-03 gained 15, 2026-11-04 moved -7, 2026-11-05 was flat at 0, and 2026-11-06 jumped 24. The first day's change is NULL - there is no previous row - and that NULL is honest: any number there would be invented. COALESCE it to 0 only if the report's readers understand it means 'no baseline', not 'no change'. LAG's optional second and third arguments (LAG(signups, 7) for a week-ago comparison, plus a default to use instead of NULL) cover most practical variations. The assumption to interrogate is that 'previous row' means 'previous day'. This table has one row per day with no gaps, so it holds. Feed LAG a table that skips weekends or missing days and it will happily compare Monday against Friday while labeling it 'yesterday'. When the calendar matters, scaffold the full date range first or join the table to itself on day = date(other.day, '+1 day'); LAG compares neighbors in the data, and only you know whether the data's neighbors are the calendar's.
Each store's sales and its percentage share of the chain total, in one result, without a separate totals query.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE store_sales (store TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO store_sales VALUES ('North', 12000), ('North', 8000), ('South', 15000), ('West', 5000)
SELECT store, SUM(amount_cents) AS store_total, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(amount_cents) / SUM(SUM(amount_cents)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_share FROM store_sales GROUP BY store ORDER BY store_total DESC

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
store	store_total	pct_share
North	20000	50.0
South	15000	37.5
West	5000	12.5

The trick is nesting: SUM(amount_cents) first aggregates rows into store totals (the GROUP BY layer), and then SUM(...) OVER () windows over those grouped results to get the chain total - an aggregate of an aggregate, which SQL permits exactly in this windowed form. Shares come out North 50.0%, South 37.5%, West 12.5%, and they sum to 100. The empty OVER () means 'the whole result set is the window' - no partitioning, no ordering - which is what a share denominator should be. Add PARTITION BY region and the same expression becomes share-of-region instead; the shape of the query is the meaning of the share, so read it before trusting a percentage in any report. Mind the arithmetic types: 100.0 * forces real division before the division happens. Written as 100 * total / grand in integer-land, SQLite would do integer division and truncate every share to a whole number - or to zero for any store under 1%. And ROUND to one decimal is presentation; keep the unrounded value around if shares must be re-aggregated, because rounded shares famously sum to 99.9 or 100.1.
For each appointment, I want the date of the same client's next appointment, to compute gaps between visits.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE appointments (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, client TEXT NOT NULL, appt_date TEXT NOT NULL)

SELECT client, appt_date, LEAD(appt_date) OVER (PARTITION BY client ORDER BY appt_date) AS next_appt, CAST(julianday(LEAD(appt_date) OVER (PARTITION BY client ORDER BY appt_date)) - julianday(appt_date) AS INTEGER) AS gap_days FROM appointments ORDER BY client, appt_date

messages.content: LEAD is LAG's forward-looking twin, and PARTITION BY client keeps each client's timeline separate - without the partition, Ana's last appointment would 'lead' into Bo's first and invent a cross-client gap. Ana's gaps come out 28 days then 42 days, and her final appointment's next_appt is NULL because the partition ends there. That trailing NULL is information, not a defect: it marks the currently-last known visit for every client, and filtering WHERE next_appt IS NULL (in an outer query, since window results cannot be filtered in the same SELECT's WHERE) is how you list each client's most recent appointment. The gap computation via julianday differences is exact for date-only values. With timestamps, the same subtraction yields fractional days - decide whether the business wants elapsed hours, calendar days, or business days, because julianday answers only the first and the other two are different functions wearing similar clothes.
Top 2 best-selling products in each category, by units sold.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE product_sales (category TEXT NOT NULL, product TEXT NOT NULL, units INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO product_sales VALUES ('paper', 'Notebook', 120), ('paper', 'Pen', 300), ('paper', 'Ruler', 45), ('kitchen', 'Mug', 150), ('kitchen', 'Kettle', 90), ('kitchen', 'Plate', 150)

SELECT category, product, units FROM (SELECT category, product, units, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY units DESC, product) AS rn FROM product_sales) WHERE rn <= 2 ORDER BY category, units DESC

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
category	product	units
kitchen	Mug	150
kitchen	Plate	150
paper	Pen	300
paper	Notebook	120

Top-N-per-group is the canonical window-function job: rank rows inside each category with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY units DESC), then filter the ranking in an outer query - the filter must live outside because window functions are computed after WHERE in the evaluation order, so the subquery (or CTE) wrapper is structural, not stylistic. The result keeps 4 rows: Mug and Plate for kitchen, Pen and Notebook for paper. The tie is the decision hiding in this query: Mug and Plate both sold 150 units, and the product-name tiebreaker in the window's ORDER BY picks Mug for rank 1 deterministically. With RANK() instead, both would be rank 1 and the filter rn <= 2 would return 3 kitchen products - sometimes exactly what 'top 2' should mean, sometimes a bug. Decide which semantics the requester wants - exactly N rows, or all rows at the top N levels - and make the tiebreaker explicit either way. An unexamined ROW_NUMBER over a non-unique ordering is a coin flip stored in a report.
Smooth our noisy daily signups with a 3-day moving average - today plus the two days before it.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE daily_signups (day TEXT PRIMARY KEY, signups INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT day, signups, ROUND(AVG(signups) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS moving_avg_3d FROM daily_signups ORDER BY day

messages.content: The frame clause is the moving part: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW makes each row's window a sliding box of up to 3 physical rows. The averages come out 40.0 on day one (a window of one - there is nothing before it), 47.5 over two days, then full 3-day windows: 47.7, 64.3, 70.0, 76.0. Note how the 90-signup spike on 2026-11-05 is absorbed into a 64.3 reading instead of dominating the chart - that dampening is the entire purpose. Two choices are embedded here and both deserve to be conscious. The head of the series uses partial windows (average of what's available); the alternative - suppressing output until 3 days exist - is a reporting decision, implemented by counting the frame and NULLing short windows. And ROWS counts rows, not days: if a date is missing from the table, the '3-day' window silently spans 4+ calendar days. For strictly calendar windows over gappy data, scaffold the dates first or use a RANGE frame over julianday values. A moving average over irregular data without that care is a precise answer to a slightly different question.
My running total changed when I switched the frame from ROWS to RANGE - same data, different numbers on the days with duplicate dates. Which one is lying?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE events (event_date TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT event_date, amount_cents, SUM(amount_cents) OVER (ORDER BY event_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rt_rows FROM events ORDER BY event_date, amount_cents DESC
SELECT event_date, amount_cents, SUM(amount_cents) OVER (ORDER BY event_date RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rt_range FROM events ORDER BY event_date, amount_cents DESC

messages.content: Neither is lying - they define 'up to me' differently. ROWS counts physical rows: the two 2026-11-03 events get running totals of 3000 and 3500, stepping one row at a time. RANGE groups peers: rows sharing the same ORDER BY value are treated as a unit, so both 11-03 rows report 3500 - the total including all of that date - because RANGE's CURRENT ROW means 'the end of my peer group'. This matters because RANGE is the default frame whenever a window has an ORDER BY: the running-total query you write casually, SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY d), is silently a RANGE query, and on data with duplicate ordering values it produces the peer-grouped version. Sometimes that is exactly right - a daily running total should arguably be constant within a day. Sometimes it corrupts a row-by-row ledger. The rule is to choose the frame by the meaning of a 'step' in your data: steps are rows (ROWS), calendar distances (RANGE over a numeric date key), or logical groups (RANGE on the natural key). Write the frame explicitly in every ordered window aggregate; inheriting the default is how this class of bug gets in.
Split our orders into four value quartiles so marketing can treat each band differently.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT id, total_cents, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY total_cents) AS quartile FROM orders ORDER BY total_cents

messages.content: NTILE(4) deals the ordered rows into four buckets as evenly as it can: with 8 orders, each quartile gets exactly 2 orders - quartile 1 runs from 900 to 1500 cents, quartile 4 from 7300 to 9900. When the count does not divide evenly, NTILE gives the extra rows to the earlier buckets, so bucket sizes differ by at most one, with the larger buckets first. Know what NTILE is not: it is not value-based binning. It splits by position, so two orders of identical value can land in different quartiles if they straddle a boundary, and a quartile boundary in a clustered dataset can separate orders one cent apart while lumping distant values together inside a sparse bucket. If marketing's bands are really value bands ('under $25, $25-50...'), a CASE expression on the amount is the honest tool; NTILE answers 'the top quarter of orders', a statement about rank, not price. Also note NTILE's result depends on the full set - adding next month's orders re-deals this month's quartiles. For stable cohort labels, compute the boundaries once and store them, rather than re-running NTILE against a growing table.
I used LAST_VALUE to get each customer's final order total of the year on every row, but it just repeats the current row's total. Is LAST_VALUE broken?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT NOT NULL, ordered_on TEXT NOT NULL, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT customer, ordered_on, LAST_VALUE(total_cents) OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY ordered_on) AS supposed_last FROM orders ORDER BY customer, ordered_on

SELECT customer, ordered_on, LAST_VALUE(total_cents) OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY ordered_on ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS actual_last FROM orders ORDER BY customer, ordered_on

messages.content: LAST_VALUE is not broken - your frame is. An ordered window's default frame ends at CURRENT ROW, so 'last value in the frame' is always the current row's own value: the naive query dutifully repeats 4000, 6200, 5100 down Ana's rows. Extending the frame to the whole partition - ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING - makes the frame's last row the partition's last row, and every Ana row now shows 5100, her November total, while Bo's rows show 8800. FIRST_VALUE never surprises people this way because the default frame starts at the partition's first row, so it works 'by accident'; LAST_VALUE is where the default frame's existence becomes visible. The general lesson: any window function whose meaning involves the frame's edges - FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTH_VALUE - demands an explicit frame decision, and aggregate windows with ORDER BY inherit a frame (RANGE up to the current peer group) whether you wrote one or not. When a window result looks like an echo of the input row, suspect the frame before the function.
Produce a dedup review table for our contacts: every duplicate email group, each row marked keep or drop, keeping the earliest signup.

| Email | Id | Signed up | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| ana@x.com | 1 | 2026-01-05 | keep |
| ana@x.com | 3 | 2026-03-19 | drop |
| ana@x.com | 6 | 2026-06-30 | drop |
| bo@x.com | 2 | 2026-02-11 | keep |
| bo@x.com | 5 | 2026-05-23 | drop |

The review covers 5 rows across the duplicated addresses: 2 keeps and 3 drops. The ranking is ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY signed_up, id) - each email's rows are numbered from its earliest signup, the id serving as a deterministic tiebreaker if two rows share a date - and rank 1 is the survivor. Presenting the decision as a reviewable table before deleting anything is the professional pattern for dedup: the query that marks is read-only, a human can eyeball the verdicts, and the eventual DELETE uses the identical ranking logic so what was reviewed is exactly what gets removed. The subquery filtering to emails with COUNT(*) > 1 keeps unique contacts out of the report entirely - they need no decision. If the survivorship rule were 'keep the most recently active' or 'keep the row with the most fields filled', only the window's ORDER BY changes; the mark-then-delete structure stays.
From a table of click timestamps per user, group clicks into sessions: a new session starts when the gap from the previous click exceeds 30 minutes.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE clicks (user_id INTEGER NOT NULL, clicked_at TEXT NOT NULL)

SELECT clicked_at, session_no FROM (SELECT clicked_at, SUM(is_start) OVER (ORDER BY clicked_at) AS session_no FROM (SELECT clicked_at, CASE WHEN prev_at IS NULL OR (julianday(clicked_at) - julianday(prev_at)) * 1440 > 30 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_start FROM (SELECT clicked_at, LAG(clicked_at) OVER (ORDER BY clicked_at) AS prev_at FROM clicks))) ORDER BY clicked_at

messages.content: Sessionization is a three-layer window construction, read from the inside out. The innermost query uses LAG to give each click its predecessor's timestamp. The middle layer turns gaps into flags: 1 when there is no predecessor or the gap - computed in minutes as the julianday difference times 1440 - exceeds 30, else 0, yielding flags at 09:00 (first), 10:20 (55 minutes after 09:25), and 12:00 (90 minutes after 10:30). The outer layer takes a running SUM of the flags, and a running sum of start-markers is exactly a session counter: 3 sessions, sized 3, 2, 1 clicks. This flag-and-cumsum pattern is one of the most reusable in analytical SQL - it also builds streaks, islands of consecutive days, and grouped sequences of any kind. The two places to be careful: the gap unit conversion (julianday speaks days; multiply deliberately and comment it), and doing this per user - with multiple users the LAG and the SUM both need PARTITION BY user_id, or one user's clicks will session-merge into another's timeline.
Where does a score of 88 sit in our exam distribution - I want a percentile-style reading for each student.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE exams (student TEXT NOT NULL, score INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO exams VALUES ('Mina', 95), ('Owen', 91), ('Priya', 88), ('Sam', 84), ('Tess', 79), ('Uma', 88)
SELECT student, score, ROUND(PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score), 2) AS pct_rank, ROUND(CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY score), 2) AS cume_dist FROM exams ORDER BY score DESC, student

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
student	score	pct_rank	cume_dist
Mina	95	1.0	1.0
Owen	91	0.8	0.83
Priya	88	0.4	0.67
Uma	88	0.4	0.67
Sam	84	0.2	0.33
Tess	79	0.0	0.17

Two distribution windows, two slightly different questions. PERCENT_RANK answers 'what fraction of the way from the lowest to the highest does this score sit', computed as (rank - 1) / (rows - 1): the top score is 1.0 by construction and the bottom is 0.0. CUME_DIST answers 'what fraction of scores are less than or equal to mine'. For the two students at 88, PERCENT_RANK gives 0.4 while CUME_DIST gives 0.67 - both are honest 'percentile-style' readings and they are not interchangeable. Ties share values in both functions, as they should: Priya and Uma are the same performance and must receive the same standing. The practical guidance: PERCENT_RANK is the closer match to the everyday word 'percentile' in these rankings, but note its edge behavior - in a class of one, it returns 0, and the top scorer is always exactly 1.0 whether they led by 1 point or 40, because rank-based measures see order, not distance. If the size of the gap matters (it usually does in score reporting), present the raw score beside the rank measure; a percentile alone can make a clustered field look spread out and a spread field look uniform.
List every order, but on each row also show that customer's lifetime total spend, so I can see each order in context without grouping the orders away.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT NOT NULL, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT id, customer, total_cents, SUM(total_cents) OVER (PARTITION BY customer) AS lifetime_cents, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY customer) AS order_count FROM orders ORDER BY customer, id

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
id	customer	total_cents	lifetime_cents	order_count
1	Ana	4000	15300	3
2	Ana	6200	15300	3
3	Ana	5100	15300	3
4	Bo	3000	11800	2
5	Bo	8800	11800	2

PARTITION BY without ORDER BY makes the window 'all rows of this customer', so the aggregate is computed per customer and then broadcast back onto each of that customer's rows: Ana's three orders each carry her lifetime total of 15300 cents and a count of 3, while Bo's rows carry 11800 over 2 orders. The detail survives - 5 rows in, 5 rows out - which is the defining difference from GROUP BY, where Ana would collapse into a single summary row and the individual orders would be gone. This broadcast pattern is the workhorse behind a family of useful columns: share of customer total (total_cents * 100.0 / the windowed sum), difference from the customer's average, 'is this their largest order' flags. One caution: the same result tempts people to filter on the windowed value in the same query ('show orders from customers worth over $100') - window functions evaluate after WHERE, so that filter needs an outer query or a CTE around this one. Structure follows evaluation order, always.
Running total of sales, but it must restart from zero at the start of each month.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE sales (sale_date TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT sale_date, amount_cents, SUM(amount_cents) OVER (PARTITION BY strftime('%Y-%m', sale_date) ORDER BY sale_date) AS month_running FROM sales ORDER BY sale_date

messages.content: PARTITION BY is the restart switch: it cuts the window into independent months, and the ordered running sum inside each partition starts fresh. October accumulates 1000 then 3000, and November begins again at 500 - the 2026-11-01 row shows its own 500 rather than 3500 - before climbing to 2700. The partition expression deserves a look: strftime('%Y-%m', sale_date) partitions by a computed value, not a stored column - windows accept expressions, so 'same month' can be defined on the fly. The same trick partitions by quarter, by week-Monday, or by any bucketing you can express. Two correctness notes. The window's ORDER BY still governs accumulation within each partition independently; partitions never leak into each other, which is the point. And if a partition key can be NULL (say, partitioning by a nullable region), all NULLs form one shared partition - usually a surprise worth checking for before the report ships.
Why can't I just replace GROUP BY with a window function everywhere and keep all my detail rows? A teammate insists windows are strictly better.

Your teammate is half right, and the half that is wrong causes real bugs. Run both on the same data: GROUP BY returns 2 rows - one per department, Kitchen totaling 5000 - because collapsing is its job. The window version returns 3 rows, every original sale, each stamped with its department's total. Different outputs, different questions: 'what did each department do' versus 'show me each sale in the context of its department'. Where windows genuinely cannot substitute: filtering and joining happen before windows in the evaluation order, so you cannot WHERE on a window result, cannot aggregate a window result further in the same SELECT (no SUM(SUM(x) OVER ...) except in the narrow grouped form), and a report that must contain exactly one row per department for a downstream join will duplicate that department once per sale if built with windows - reintroducing fan-out through the back door. There is also a compositional truth: window functions are evaluated after GROUP BY, so the two are layers, not rivals - several queries in this corpus window over grouped results to compute shares of totals. Learn the evaluation order (FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, windows, ORDER BY) and the choice stops being a matter of taste: the layer that can express your question is the layer you use.
Show me the orders that are bigger than the average order - I need the actual order rows, not just a count.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT NOT NULL, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT AVG(total_cents) AS avg_total FROM orders
SELECT id, customer, total_cents FROM orders WHERE total_cents > (SELECT AVG(total_cents) FROM orders) ORDER BY total_cents DESC

messages.content: A scalar subquery is a query that returns exactly one value, and here it plays the role of a computed constant: the average order is 5920.0 cents, and the outer query keeps the 2 orders above it - Dee's 12000-cent order leads. The subquery is uncorrelated: it does not reference the outer table, so conceptually it is evaluated once and the comparison is then a simple per-row test. Why not compute the average in your application code and pass it in as a literal? Sometimes that is fine, but the subquery keeps the definition of 'average' inside the query where it belongs: if the table changes between the two steps of a code-side version, the threshold and the rows can disagree, and a reader of the SQL sees the whole rule in one place. The failure mode to know: a scalar subquery that returns more than one row is a runtime error, and one that returns zero rows yields NULL - making every comparison UNKNOWN and the result silently empty. When you write one, convince yourself it returns exactly one row by construction (an aggregate without GROUP BY always does), not by hope about the current data.
I need the list of customers who have at least one shipped order. A JOIN gives me some customers three times. A colleague says use IN instead - why does that change the result?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id), status TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'Ana'), (2, 'Bo'), (3, 'Cy')
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (11, 1, 'shipped'), (12, 1, 'shipped'), (13, 1, 'pending'), (14, 2, 'shipped'), (15, 3, 'pending')
SELECT c.name FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.status = 'shipped' ORDER BY c.name
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped') ORDER BY name

messages.content: The JOIN version returns 3 rows - Ana twice, once for each of her shipped orders - because a join's grain is the pair, not the customer. The IN version returns 2 rows: Ana and Bo, each once, because IN asks a membership question about each customer - 'is your id in this set?' - which is true or false, never 'twice true'. The two queries answer different questions that happen to share words. 'Customers with at least one shipped order' is a membership question about customers, so its grain is customers and IN (or EXISTS) is the natural tool. 'Show me the shipped orders with customer names' is a pairing question, and the JOIN with its repeated names is correct there. You can patch the JOIN with DISTINCT, and for this simple case it works - but it papers over the grain mismatch and gets fragile as soon as the SELECT list grows columns that legitimately differ per order. Choose the construct whose grain matches the question and the duplicates never appear, rather than deduplicating a result that was built at the wrong grain.
Bizarre bug: WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM legacy_orders) returns zero rows even though most customers have no legacy orders. The IN version works fine.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE legacy_orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER)
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'Ana'), (2, 'Bo'), (3, 'Cy')
INSERT INTO legacy_orders VALUES (11, 1), (12, NULL)
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM legacy_orders) ORDER BY name
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM legacy_orders) ORDER BY name
SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM legacy_orders l WHERE l.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY name

messages.content: The legacy_orders table contains a NULL customer_id, and that single NULL poisons NOT IN completely. NOT IN unfolds to 'id <> every value in the list': for Bo, that is (2 <> 1) AND (2 <> NULL) - the second comparison is UNKNOWN, true AND unknown is unknown, and Bo is filtered out. Every customer fails the same way, so the result is 0 rows, while the positive IN still finds Ana (1 row) because a single TRUE is enough for IN regardless of the UNKNOWNs. NOT EXISTS is immune: it asks whether a matching row exists, and a NULL customer_id simply never matches, so the fixed query correctly returns Bo, Cy. The rule is absolute: never use NOT IN with a subquery whose selected column can contain NULL - and 'can' means by schema, not by today's data, because the bug activates the day the first NULL lands. Either use NOT EXISTS, or filter the subquery with WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL and accept the fragility. NOT EXISTS also tends to optimize better, since the engine can stop at the first match. This is the single most destructive NULL behavior in everyday SQL; it returns an empty set with no error, looking exactly like 'no rows qualify'.

This is a correlated subquery: the inner query references c.id from the outer row, so it is re-evaluated for each customer, returning that customer's maximum order date - Ana 2026-11-02, Bo 2026-10-19 - and for Cy, who has no orders, MAX over an empty set yields NULL, so she appears with a blank rather than disappearing. This nested query works but nobody can read it: months whose signups beat the average month, where months are themselves aggregated from raw signups. Rewrite it readably and prove the answer does not change.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE signups (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, signed_on TEXT NOT NULL)

SELECT month, n FROM (SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', signed_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS n FROM signups GROUP BY month) WHERE n > (SELECT AVG(n) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM signups GROUP BY strftime('%Y-%m', signed_on))) ORDER BY month
WITH monthly AS (SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', signed_on) AS month, COUNT(*) AS n FROM signups GROUP BY month) SELECT month, n FROM monthly WHERE n > (SELECT AVG(n) FROM monthly) ORDER BY month

messages.content: Both forms return the same 1 month - 2026-09 with 4 signups, against an average month of 3. The CTE version defines monthly once, names it, and then reads like the sentence it implements: compute monthly counts, keep the months above the average of those counts. The nested version computes the identical aggregation twice, inline, in two different syntactic corners, and a reader must verify the two copies agree before trusting either. That duplication is the real argument for CTEs beyond readability: in the nested form, editing the bucketing logic (say, switching to weekly) requires finding and changing both copies, and changing only one produces a query that runs fine and answers a question nobody asked. A CTE is not automatically faster - SQLite may inline or materialize it depending on version and shape - and it is not a temp table; it lives for one statement. Reach for it when a query has stages a human would name: extract, aggregate, compare, present. If you can name the stages, the WITH clause is where the names go.
Print the org chart with each person's depth in the hierarchy - CEO at depth 0, her reports at 1, and so on.

INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1, 'Marla', NULL), (2, 'Ana', 1), (3, 'Bo', 1), (4, 'Cy', 2), (5, 'Dee', 2), (6, 'Eli', 4)

WITH RECURSIVE org(id, name, depth) AS (SELECT id, name, 0 FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.name, o.depth + 1 FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id) SELECT name, depth FROM org ORDER BY depth, name

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	depth
Marla	0
Ana	1
Bo	1
Cy	2
Dee	2
Eli	3

A recursive CTE walks a self-referencing table the way a person would: start from the anchor - the employee with no manager, Marla at depth 0 - then repeatedly join the employees table against the rows found so far, adding one depth level per hop. The walk visits all 6 employees and bottoms out at depth 3 with Eli, who reports to Cy, who reports to Ana, who reports to Marla. The two halves have distinct jobs and distinct failure modes. The anchor (before UNION ALL) seeds the recursion and must select exactly the roots - if two executives had NULL managers, both would correctly start trees at depth 0. The recursive step must join on the parent link (e.manager_id = org.id); join it backwards and the walk explodes upward or returns nothing. The mortal danger is a cycle: if data corruption ever made Ana manage Marla, the recursion would loop until SQLite's limits stop it, producing garbage rather than an error. Production hierarchies guard with a depth cap in the recursive step (WHERE depth < 50) - cheap insurance that turns an infinite walk into a visibly truncated one you can investigate.

A cart assembly needs 2 wheel subassemblies; each wheel needs 1 hub and 4 bolts; each hub needs 5 screws. How many total parts, by part, to build one cart? The parts table lists what each assembly directly contains.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE bom (parent TEXT NOT NULL, component TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO bom VALUES ('cart', 'wheel', 2), ('cart', 'frame', 1), ('wheel', 'hub', 1), ('wheel', 'bolt', 4), ('hub', 'screw', 5), ('frame', 'bolt', 6)

WITH RECURSIVE need(part, qty) AS (SELECT component, qty FROM bom WHERE parent = 'cart' UNION ALL SELECT b.component, n.qty * b.qty FROM need n JOIN bom b ON b.parent = n.part) SELECT part, SUM(qty) AS total_qty FROM need GROUP BY part ORDER BY part

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
part	total_qty
bolt	14
frame	1
hub	2
screw	10
wheel	2

This is a bill-of-materials explosion, and the recursive step carries a multiplier: each need row expands into its components with quantities multiplied by how many of the parent are needed. The walk generates wheels (2), their hubs (2 x 1 = 2) and bolts (2 x 4 = 8), the hubs' screws (2 x 5 = 10), and the frame's own bolts (6) - and because bolt arrives by two paths, the final GROUP BY sums them to 14. Total distinct parts: 5, with 2 wheels, 2 hubs, 1 frame, 14 bolts, 10 screws. Two properties make this work where a fixed-depth join cannot: the recursion discovers the tree's depth from the data (add a sub-subassembly and nothing in the query changes), and UNION ALL - not UNION - is essential, because the same part legitimately appears on multiple paths and deduplication would undercount before the SUM. The corresponding hazard is the mirror image: a cyclic BOM (a part that contains itself, directly or through a loop) recurses forever, multiplying as it goes. Real BOM systems validate acyclicity on write; the depth-cap guard from org charts applies here too. Recursion in SQL is a power tool: exact, elegant, and entirely dependent on the tree actually being a tree.

The cost is evaluation per row: the subquery runs once per customer, so on very large tables the join form usually wins on speed, and an index on orders(customer_id) is what makes either acceptable. Which of our suppliers have no products in the catalog at all? I need the missing-counterpart list for a purchasing review.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE suppliers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, supplier_id INTEGER REFERENCES suppliers(id), name TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO suppliers VALUES (1, 'Acme'), (2, 'Beacon'), (3, 'Corvid'), (4, 'Dune')
INSERT INTO products VALUES (11, 1, 'Widget'), (12, 1, 'Gadget'), (13, 3, 'Sprocket'), (14, NULL, 'Unattributed sample')
SELECT s.name FROM suppliers s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM products p WHERE p.supplier_id = s.id) ORDER BY s.name

messages.content: An anti-join finds rows with no counterpart, and NOT EXISTS states it most directly: keep suppliers for whom no product row claims them. The answer is Beacon, Dune - 2 of the 4 suppliers supply nothing in the catalog. Notice the unattributed sample product, whose supplier_id is NULL: it correctly counts for nobody, since NULL never equals any supplier id inside the EXISTS check. That is exactly the behavior you want, and it is where the alternative anti-join spellings diverge in risk: LEFT JOIN ... WHERE p.id IS NULL gives the same result here, but NOT IN (SELECT supplier_id FROM products) would have returned zero rows, poisoned by that same NULL - the trap demonstrated elsewhere in this corpus. Anti-joins are the natural language of data-quality work: orders with no customer, payments with no invoice, files with no metadata row. Learn to hear 'which X have no Y' as NOT EXISTS with a correlated inner query, and reach for the other spellings only with a reason.
Generate a 6-month payoff schedule for a $1,200 loan at $220/month: month number, payment, and remaining balance - the table has no schedule rows, I need SQL to manufacture them.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE loan (principal_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, payment_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO loan VALUES (120000, 22000)

WITH RECURSIVE seq(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM seq WHERE n < 6) SELECT n AS month, MIN((SELECT payment_cents FROM loan), (SELECT principal_cents FROM loan) - (n - 1) * (SELECT payment_cents FROM loan)) AS payment, MAX((SELECT principal_cents FROM loan) - n * (SELECT payment_cents FROM loan), 0) AS balance_after FROM seq ORDER BY n

messages.content: A recursive CTE doubles as a series generator: the anchor emits 1, the recursive step keeps adding 1 while n < 6, and suddenly SQL has the integers 1..6 to compute against - no calendar or sequence table required. The schedule runs five full payments of 22000 cents and a final smaller one of 10000 cents in month 6, because MIN caps the last payment at what is actually owed, and the balance after month 6 reaches 0. The MAX(..., 0) on the balance is the same defensive idea at the other end: without it, a schedule longer than the payoff would print negative balances - arithmetic faithfully extending a model past its domain. Generated series plus edge clamps is the honest way to model in SQL: compute the ideal line, then clamp it to reality at the boundaries. This generator pattern - dates, months, numbers - is also how calendar scaffolds are built for gap-filling reports. Whenever a query needs rows that reality has not provided (future months, empty days, sequence numbers), a recursive CTE is the factory.
WHERE discount_code = NULL returns no rows even though plenty of orders have no discount code. Am I querying wrong?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, discount_code TEXT, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'SAVE10', 5000), (2, NULL, 3000), (3, NULL, 4500), (4, 'FREESHIP', 6000)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS with_equals_null FROM orders WHERE discount_code = NULL
SELECT id, total_cents FROM orders WHERE discount_code IS NULL ORDER BY id

messages.content: You are querying the way every newcomer does, and SQL's NULL rules are the obstacle. NULL is not a value - it is the absence of one - so the comparison discount_code = NULL never evaluates to true for any row; it evaluates to UNKNOWN, because 'is this missing thing equal to that missing thing' has no answer. Your count comes back 0, always, on every table, forever. NULL gets its own operators: IS NULL finds the 2 orders with no code (ids 2 and 3), and IS NOT NULL finds the rest. Internalize the model and a dozen other puzzles dissolve at once: any comparison involving NULL yields UNKNOWN (except the IS tests), WHERE keeps only TRUE, and arithmetic on NULL yields NULL. SQL is not being pedantic - it is refusing to invent facts about data that is not there. Your job is to ask about absence with the tools built for absence.
My invoice total comes out blank whenever one line has a missing quantity. The math is just qty * price summed up - why does one missing value kill the whole total?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE invoice_lines (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, qty INTEGER, unit_price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO invoice_lines VALUES (1, 2, 1500), (2, NULL, 2000), (3, 1, 500)
SELECT qty * unit_price_cents AS line_total FROM invoice_lines ORDER BY id
SELECT SUM(qty * unit_price_cents) AS naive_total, SUM(COALESCE(qty, 0) * unit_price_cents) AS total_qty0, SUM(COALESCE(qty, 1) * unit_price_cents) AS total_qty1 FROM invoice_lines

messages.content: NULL propagates through arithmetic: 2 * 1500 is 3000, but NULL * 2000 is NULL - an unknown quantity times a known price is an unknown amount, and the per-line output shows the hole directly. SUM then ignores that NULL line, so the naive total is 3500 cents - not blank in this case, but silently short: it prices the missing-quantity line at nothing while pretending to be the invoice total. The two COALESCE variants make the business decision explicit: treating the missing quantity as 0 gives 3500 cents (same number, but now it is a stated policy, not an accident), while treating it as 1 gives 5500. The lesson is that 'what should a missing quantity mean' is a business question the database cannot answer, and the danger is not the NULL itself but the silent default: SUM's NULL-skipping turned a data problem into a plausible-looking wrong total. Where a missing input should be loud, guard for it - a COUNT check for NULLs, or a constraint - and where it should be absorbed, COALESCE at the exact term that is missing, so the policy is visible in the query text.
One product's average rating shows blank even though it has reviews. The reviews are all there - I can see them. Why is the average empty?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE reviews (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product TEXT NOT NULL, rating INTEGER)
INSERT INTO reviews VALUES (1, 'Kettle', 5), (2, 'Kettle', 4), (3, 'Lamp', NULL), (4, 'Lamp', NULL), (5, 'Mug', 3)
SELECT product, AVG(rating) AS avg_rating, COUNT(rating) AS rated, COUNT(*) AS reviews FROM reviews GROUP BY product ORDER BY product

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
product	avg_rating	rated	reviews
Kettle	4.5	2	2
Lamp	NULL	0	2
Mug	3.0	1	1

Lamp has 2 reviews and 0 ratings: every one of its rating fields is NULL - the review text arrived, the stars never did. Aggregates over a set with no actual values return NULL, so Lamp's average is blank while Kettle's 4.5 and Mug's 3.0 compute normally. An average of nothing is not zero; it is undefined, and SQL says so with NULL. This is the aggregate counterpart of the propagation rule: SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX over zero non-NULL inputs all return NULL (COUNT is the exception - it happily returns 0, which is how you detect this situation). For display, COALESCE(avg_rating, 0) is a lie of commission - it would rank an unrated product beside a product rated zero stars, if zero were even possible. The honest presentations are 'not yet rated' (COALESCE to a label in the presentation layer) or excluding the product from ranked lists until COUNT(rating) > 0. When a stakeholder asks why a number is missing, the missingness is usually the finding: here, a ratings pipeline is dropping stars for one product, and the blank average is the smoke, not the fire.
I want all orders that are not cancelled: WHERE NOT (status = 'cancelled'). But orders whose status was never set are missing from the result too.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, status TEXT)
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'shipped'), (2, 'cancelled'), (3, NULL), (4, 'pending'), (5, NULL)
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE NOT (status = 'cancelled') ORDER BY id
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE status IS NOT 'cancelled' ORDER BY id
SELECT COUNT(*) AS with_or FROM orders WHERE NOT (status = 'cancelled') OR status IS NULL

messages.content: Three-valued logic strikes: for the NULL-status orders, status = 'cancelled' is UNKNOWN, NOT UNKNOWN is still UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE - so your query returns 2 orders and silently drops ids 3 and 5 along with the cancelled one. The fixed query using IS NOT returns 4 rows: IS NOT is NULL-aware inequality, true whenever the value is not 'cancelled', including when there is no value. The OR status IS NULL spelling reaches the same 4 and is the portable form for databases without IS NOT. The general shape of this bug: any negated condition - NOT (...), <> , NOT IN - applied to a nullable column loses the NULL rows, because negation does not turn UNKNOWN into TRUE. 'Not cancelled' in business language almost always means 'everything except cancelled, including unset'; SQL hears it as 'known to be something else'. Audit your WHERE clauses for negations over nullable columns the way you audit for NOT IN: each one needs a deliberate decision about the NULL population, written into the query where the next reader can see it.
Our users table has a UNIQUE constraint on email, yet two rows with no email got in. Is the constraint broken? And can a third get in?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT UNIQUE)
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'ana@x.com')
INSERT INTO users VALUES (2, NULL)
INSERT INTO users VALUES (3, NULL)
INSERT INTO users VALUES (4, 'ana@x.com')
SELECT id, email FROM users ORDER BY id

messages.content: The constraint is working exactly as SQL defines it - and the definition surprises people. A UNIQUE constraint forbids two equal values, but NULLs are never equal to anything, not even each other, so each NULL email is 'unique' by vacuity. Both NULL inserts succeeded, giving 3 rows, while the genuine duplicate 'ana@x.com' was rejected with a UNIQUE constraint failure, as the failed fourth insert shows. A third NULL can get in too, and a thirtieth. Whether that is a bug depends on intent: if email is optional-but-unique-when-present (multiple staff accounts without email, one per real address), the behavior is precisely right. If every user must have an email, the schema needs NOT NULL beside the UNIQUE - uniqueness was never the rule that guaranteed presence. Dialect warning: this is SQLite and standard-SQL behavior, and PostgreSQL agrees by default, but some databases historically treated NULLs as equal for uniqueness and allowed only one. When a schema must behave identically across engines, do not rely on the default - state presence with NOT NULL and uniqueness with UNIQUE, as separate, explicit decisions.

Conversion rate per campaign is clicks divided into conversions, but one campaign has zero clicks and the report either errors or shows nonsense depending on the tool. Make it robust.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE campaigns (name TEXT NOT NULL, clicks INTEGER NOT NULL, conversions INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO campaigns VALUES ('Spring', 200, 25), ('Summer', 0, 0), ('Fall', 150, 30)
SELECT name, clicks, conversions, ROUND(100.0 * conversions / NULLIF(clicks, 0), 1) AS conv_rate_pct FROM campaigns ORDER BY name

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	clicks	conversions	conv_rate_pct
Fall	150	30	20.0
Spring	200	25	12.5
Summer	0	0	NULL

NULLIF(clicks, 0) is the guard: it returns NULL when clicks is 0 and clicks otherwise, turning the dangerous division into conversions / NULL, which yields NULL instead of an error or an infinity. Summer's rate therefore shows as NULL - undefined, which is the truth for a campaign nobody clicked - while Spring computes 12.5% and Fall 20.0%. In SQLite bare division by zero actually returns NULL rather than raising, but the same query in stricter engines aborts the whole report, and in spreadsheet-adjacent tools produces the nonsense you saw. Writing the NULLIF makes the intent portable and explicit: this rate does not exist when there were no clicks. Then decide the presentation separately: a dashboard might COALESCE the NULL to 0 for sorting, but that conflates 'no traffic' with 'traffic that never converted' - two situations demanding opposite responses (fix the campaign's reach versus fix its landing page). NULLIF plus a deliberate display choice keeps the statistic honest at both layers. The same pattern guards per-capita rates, averages of ratios, and any division whose denominator is data rather than a constant.

INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'Ana'), (2, 'Bo')
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (11, 1, 5000), (12, NULL, 3000), (13, 2, 4500), (14, NULL, 2750)

messages.content: The two unmatchable orders have customer_id NULL - visible in the orphan query as ids 12 and 14, worth 3000 and 2750 cents. A NULL foreign key can never join, because the join tests customer_id = customers.id and NULL = anything is UNKNOWN, never TRUE - NULL does not match even another NULL, so there is no customer row in the universe, real or placeholder, that these orders can pair with. What not to do is paper over it with a fake 'Unknown Customer' row and point the orphans at it without a decision - that converts a visible data problem into invisible wrong attribution.

It did, and by the standard's design: a CHECK constraint rejects a row only when its condition evaluates to FALSE. Give me a reference table I can pin above my desk: the common NULL expressions and what each actually evaluates to in SQLite.

| Expression | Evaluates to |
|---|---|
| NULL = NULL | NULL |
| NULL IS NULL | 1 |
| NULL <> 5 | NULL |
| NULL + 5 | NULL |
| NULL || 'text' | NULL |
| COALESCE(NULL, 'fallback') | fallback |
| NULLIF(5, 5) | NULL |
| COUNT of one NULL | 0 |
| NULL IN (1, 2) | NULL |
| 5 NOT IN (1, NULL) | NULL |

Read the pattern, not just the rows. Anything that compares or computes with NULL produces NULL (UNKNOWN for comparisons, absent for arithmetic and concatenation), because SQL will not invent a value for missing data. The exceptions are the tools built specifically for absence: IS NULL answers the question directly with 1, COALESCE substitutes a fallback, and NULLIF manufactures a NULL on purpose when two values match - the division guard. The two rows that bite in production are the quiet ones: NULL || 'text' returning NULL means one missing name part erases a whole concatenated label, and 5 NOT IN (1, NULL) returning NULL (filtered out as not-true) is the NOT IN poison in miniature. Keep this table nearby until the reflex forms: when a column can be NULL, every expression touching it has a NULL case, and the time to decide that case is when you write the query.

Our product list is paged 3 at a time, sorted by price. Show me page 2.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE products (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)

SELECT name, price_cents FROM products ORDER BY price_cents, id LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3

messages.content: LIMIT caps how many rows come back and OFFSET skips rows before the cap starts counting, so page 2 is LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3 over the same ordering: Ruler (450), Notebook (1200), Mug (1500). Page 1, for reference, ended with Pen at 300 cents, and page 2 picks up exactly where it left off. The load-bearing detail is the ORDER BY - and specifically that it ends with id. Prices tie in real catalogs, and OFFSET/LIMIT slices the ordered stream at fixed positions; if the order among tied prices is unspecified, the database may arrange ties differently between the page-1 query and the page-2 query, and an item can appear on both pages or on neither. A unique final sort key makes the ordering total, and a total ordering makes pages a true partition. The formula generalizes: page N at size S is LIMIT S OFFSET (N-1)*S. Keep the ordering identical across pages - same columns, same direction - because the pages are slices of one logical list, not separate queries that happen to look alike.

Users report seeing the same item twice while paging through the catalog, and another item never appears at all. Nothing is wrong with the data - it changes while they browse. Demonstrate the mechanism.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE catalog (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO catalog VALUES (1, 'Eraser', 150), (2, 'Pencil', 200), (3, 'Pen', 300), (4, 'Ruler', 450), (5, 'Notebook', 1200), (6, 'Mug', 1500)
SELECT name FROM catalog ORDER BY price_cents, id LIMIT 3

messages.content: Watch the two pages overlap. Page 1, fetched before the insert, was Eraser, Pencil, Pen. A new 100-cent Glue Stick then enters the catalog and sorts to the very front, pushing every existing row one position down - so page 2, fetched a moment later with OFFSET 3, starts one row earlier in the original sequence and serves Pen a second time, while the last row of the old ordering slides onto a page 3 the user may never open. OFFSET does not remember what it showed you; it counts positions in the current ordering at fetch time. Any insertion or deletion ahead of the window shifts every subsequent page. The busier the table, the more duplicates and skips accumulate, and no bug exists in any single query - the instability is a property of position-based addressing over mutable data. This is why feeds and APIs that page over live data prefer keyset pagination (next page = 'rows after this last-seen key'), which anchors to values instead of positions. OFFSET remains perfectly fine for static data, exports, and admin tables where a shifted row costs nothing - the sin is using it where the ground moves.

Keyset paging throws away positions and keeps a cursor: the last row of page 1 was Pen, price 300, id 3 - so page 2 is 'rows whose (price, id) sorts strictly after (300, 3)', expressed as the row-value comparison (price_cents, id) > (300, 3). SELECT id, label FROM feed ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 2
SELECT id, label FROM feed ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2
SELECT id, label FROM feed ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT 2 OFFSET 4

messages.content: Three of the five events share the timestamp 09:00, so 'ORDER BY created_at' alone defines only a partial order: within the tie, the database may return login, click, scroll in any arrangement, and the arrangement can differ between the page-1 query and the page-2 query - an event straddling the boundary can be served twice or not at all, with no data changing at all. The fix is a total order: ORDER BY created_at, id makes every row's position unique and stable, and the three pages then partition the feed exactly - ids [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] across pages, each event precisely once. This is the same disease as OFFSET drift with a different cause: drift comes from the data moving, tie instability comes from the order itself being underdetermined. Both are cured by anchoring pages to something unique and immutable about each row. The rule to internalize: any ORDER BY used for paging, ranking, or top-N must end in a unique key. Timestamps are almost never unique in event data - batch jobs and same-second writes guarantee collisions - so the primary key (or another monotonic value like a sequence number) is not an optional garnish on the sort; it is the part that makes the sort a sort.
