The tangle usually comes from mixing the two comparisons into separate AND/OR clauses by hand and losing the tie case: rows equal on created_at but past the cursor on id. The row-value form (created_at, id) < (?, ?) handles both components lexicographically in one expression and mirrors the ORDER BY exactly - whatever the sort key tuple is, the cursor predicate is that same tuple compared with the direction of travel. Mnemonic: the predicate points the way the pages flow. Ascending flow, > cursor; descending flow, < cursor; and the tuple is always the full sort key, never just its first column.
The UI needs 'page X of Y'. Given the product count and a page size of 4, compute the total number of pages in SQL - including the awkward case where the count divides unevenly.

The expression (count + size - 1) / size is integer ceiling division: adding size - 1 before dividing pushes any partial group over the next whole boundary, so 9 items become (9 + 3) / 4 = 3 - two full pages and a third holding the remaining 1 item, which the last-page query confirms. Why not just divide and round? Because the pieces conspire: in SQLite, 9 / 4 is integer division and yields 2, discarding the remainder that represents real products; CASTing to REAL and using CEIL works but drags floating point into a counting problem that integers solve exactly. The (n + s - 1) / s idiom is exact for all counts, including the edge cases - 8 items give exactly 2 pages, and 0 items give 0 pages, which is the answer a UI wants before it renders 'page 1 of 0' nonsense. Pair this with the paging queries themselves: same page size constant everywhere, and derive the current page's slice from the same ORDER BY discipline, so the 'of Y' the UI promises is the Y the queries can actually deliver.

SELECT signed_on, COUNT(*) AS n FROM signups GROUP BY signed_on ORDER BY signed_on

WITH RECURSIVE days(d) AS (SELECT '2026-11-02' UNION ALL SELECT date(d, '+1 day') FROM days WHERE d < '2026-11-06') SELECT d AS day, COUNT(s.id) AS signups FROM days LEFT JOIN signups s ON s.signed_on = d GROUP BY d ORDER BY d

messages.content: The raw grouping returns 3 rows because a group can only form around a date that exists in the data. The filled version generates the calendar first - a recursive CTE stepping day by day from 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-06 - and LEFT JOINs the signups onto it, so all 5 days appear and 2026-11-03, 2026-11-05 show an honest 0. COUNT(s.id) rather than COUNT(*) is what makes the zeros real: the padded rows have NULL signup columns, and counting a column ignores them, while COUNT(*) would report 1 for every empty day - the phantom-count trap from LEFT JOIN aggregation. This scaffold pattern is the general answer to 'the series has holes': generate the complete axis (days, weeks, months), attach facts with a LEFT JOIN, and let absence render as zero. The axis boundaries are parameters of the report - pass the range in rather than deriving it from MIN/MAX of the data, or a range that starts before the first sale will silently shrink to the data's own start and hide exactly the emptiness you were asked to show.
Events are stored as UTC timestamps, but the business reports by Eastern days. An event at 02:30 UTC is still the previous evening here. Show me how the day counts change when I bucket by local day.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE events (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, ts_utc TEXT NOT NULL, kind TEXT NOT NULL)
SELECT date(ts_utc) AS utc_day, COUNT(*) AS n FROM events GROUP BY utc_day ORDER BY utc_day
SELECT date(ts_utc, '-5 hours') AS local_day, COUNT(*) AS n FROM events GROUP BY local_day ORDER BY local_day

messages.content: Bucketing by the raw UTC date gives 2026-11-03: 3 events and 2026-11-04: 2. Shifting each timestamp back 5 hours before taking the date - date(ts_utc, '-5 hours'), using a fixed Eastern Standard offset - moves the boundary: event 1 at 02:30 UTC becomes 21:30 on Nov 2 local, and event 4 at 04:45 UTC becomes 23:45 on Nov 3 local, so the local buckets read 2026-11-02: 1, 2026-11-03: 3, 2026-11-04: 1. Same five events, genuinely different daily numbers - neither is wrong; they answer to different definitions of 'day'. The fixed -5 hours offset is the deliberate simplification here, and its limit must be stated: Eastern alternates between -5 (EST) and -4 (EDT), so a fixed offset misfiles events by an hour around the daylight-saving transitions and for the whole summer if the business means wall-clock Eastern. SQLite's own 'localtime' modifier uses the server's timezone, which is a deployment fact, not a business rule. The robust architectures are to store the local date (or the offset) alongside the UTC instant at write time, or to bucket in the application layer with a real timezone database. What you must never do is mix definitions - some reports UTC, some local - because the totals will disagree by exactly the near-midnight events and nobody will trust either.
Group members into age bands - under 18, 18-29, 30-44, 45-64, 65+ - and count each band, from birth dates.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE members (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, born_on TEXT NOT NULL)

SELECT CASE WHEN age < 18 THEN 'under 18' WHEN age < 30 THEN '18-29' WHEN age < 45 THEN '30-44' WHEN age < 65 THEN '45-64' ELSE '65+' END AS band, COUNT(*) AS members FROM (SELECT CAST((julianday('2026-11-27') - julianday(born_on)) / 365.25 AS INTEGER) AS age FROM members) GROUP BY band ORDER BY MIN(age)

messages.content: The pattern is compute-then-bucket: an inner query derives each member's age in years (the julianday difference divided by 365.25, truncated - the standard approximation that handles leap years on average), and a CASE in the outer query maps the age to its band label, first matching WHEN wins. The bands come out under 18: 1, 18-29: 3, 30-44: 2, 45-64: 1, 65+: 1 - all 5 bands populated from the 8 members. Order the WHENs from the most specific boundary upward and let each test be a simple '<' - overlapping or gappy ranges are the classic CASE bug, and the ascending-threshold ladder makes both impossible to write by accident: every age lands in exactly one band because the tests partition the number line. Two honest caveats. The 365.25 division can be off by a day around a birthday, so for eligibility decisions ('is this member 18 today') compute with date arithmetic against the exact anniversary instead; for demographic banding the approximation is fine and standard. And sorting bands by MIN(age) rather than by label keeps 'under 18' first - alphabetical order would scatter the bands ('18-29', '30-44', '45-64', '65+', 'under 18'), a small chart crime committed daily.
Cohort check: for customers who first ordered in September and in October, how many placed another order in the month right after their first?

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer TEXT NOT NULL, ordered_on TEXT NOT NULL)

WITH firsts AS (SELECT customer, MIN(ordered_on) AS first_on, strftime('%Y-%m', MIN(ordered_on)) AS cohort FROM orders GROUP BY customer) SELECT f.cohort, COUNT(*) AS cohort_size, SUM(CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer = f.customer AND strftime('%Y-%m', o.ordered_on) = strftime('%Y-%m', f.first_on, '+1 month')) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS returned_next_month FROM firsts f GROUP BY f.cohort ORDER BY f.cohort

messages.content: Cohort analysis starts by stamping each customer with their cohort - the month of their first order, computed once in the firsts CTE via MIN(ordered_on). Retention is then an EXISTS question per customer: did any order land in the calendar month after the first, computed with date arithmetic on the cohort month rather than on raw day differences. September's cohort has 3 customers of whom 1 returned in October; October's cohort has 2 with 1 returning in November. Eli is the instructive exclusion: his second order came in November, two months after his September debut - a returning customer, but not a next-month return, and the cohort metric correctly does not count him. Retention windows are definitions, and the query is the definition written down; change '+1 month' and you change the metric, so the expression belongs in the report's methodology note. Structurally, note the division of labor: the CTE establishes one row per customer with the cohort attribute, and the conditional SUM over an EXISTS flag counts successes without ever joining orders to orders at full grain - the shape stays readable and the fan-out traps stay out.
Two ways to count November orders: strftime on the date column, or a date-range predicate. A senior dev says one of them can't use the index on ordered_on. Verify they agree, and explain.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, ordered_on TEXT NOT NULL, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS via_function FROM orders WHERE strftime('%Y-%m', ordered_on) = '2026-11'
SELECT COUNT(*) AS via_range FROM orders WHERE ordered_on >= '2026-11-01' AND ordered_on < '2026-12-01'

messages.content: They agree exactly: both count 3 November orders, excluding the Oct 31 and Dec 1 boundary rows. The difference is not the answer but the cost of finding it. The range predicate compares the stored column directly against constants, so an index on ordered_on can seek straight to '2026-11-01' and scan only November's slice - the predicate is sargable. The strftime version wraps the column in a function: the database must compute the function for every row to know whether it matches, because the index is built on the raw values, not on their strftime images - a full scan wearing a filter's clothes. The rule of thumb: never wrap the column you want indexed in a function inside WHERE; transform the constant side instead. 'ordered_on >= first-of-month AND ordered_on < first-of-next-month' keeps the column bare. The half-open interval (< next month, not <= last day) also dodges the month-length question entirely - November 30 vs 31 never enters into it, and timestamps with times behave correctly too. Function-wrapped columns are fine in SELECT and GROUP BY, where they shape output after rows are chosen. In WHERE they silently retire your indexes, and the query still returns the right answer - which is exactly why the habit survives code review unless someone is watching for it.
For each day, the total sales of the trailing 7 days ending that day (a rolling weekly total, not a calendar-week total).

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE sales (sale_date TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)

SELECT d.sale_date, (SELECT SUM(s.amount_cents) FROM sales s WHERE s.sale_date BETWEEN date(d.sale_date, '-6 days') AND d.sale_date) AS trailing_7d FROM (SELECT DISTINCT sale_date FROM sales) d ORDER BY d.sale_date

messages.content: A trailing window is a range condition, not a row count, so the honest construction is a per-day range sum: for each distinct sale date, sum every sale whose date falls in [day - 6, day]. The series builds as 1000 on Nov 1, 3000 by Nov 3, 4500 by Nov 5 - then Nov 8's window (Nov 2..Nov 8) has aged out the Nov 1 sale, giving 6500, and Nov 9 totals 7000. The aging-out is visible in the numbers: the total falls even though Nov 8 outsold every prior day, because Nov 1 left the window. Contrast with the ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING window-function version: that sums the previous 7 rows, and this table has gaps (no sales Nov 2, 4, 6, 7), so '7 rows back' reaches much further than 7 days back. Rows are not days - the same lesson as the moving-average case, now with money attached. A window-function formulation does exist (RANGE over a julianday expression), but the correlated range-sum states the semantics in plain sight and works on any engine. Its cost is a scan per output day, fine at report scale; at very large scale you would scaffold a complete calendar and use a running difference of cumulative sums - two window passes, constant work per row.
Monthly revenue split by payment method - card, cash, and transfer as columns - with a total column that must reconcile.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE payments (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, method TEXT NOT NULL, paid_on TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)

SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', paid_on) AS month, SUM(CASE WHEN method = 'card' THEN amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS card, SUM(CASE WHEN method = 'cash' THEN amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS cash, SUM(CASE WHEN method = 'transfer' THEN amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS transfer, SUM(amount_cents) AS total FROM payments GROUP BY month ORDER BY month

messages.content: Conditional aggregation over amounts rather than counts: each CASE routes a payment's amount into exactly one method column, and the unconditioned SUM(amount_cents) stands as the reconciliation witness. October reads card 8000, cash 2000, transfer 0, total 10000; November reads card 4500, cash 1500, transfer 9500, total 15500 - and in both rows the three method columns sum exactly to the total. That reconciliation is not a nicety; it is the pivot's proof of correctness. The failure it catches is the unanticipated category: the day a 'wallet' payment first appears, it lands in the total but in no column, and the row stops adding up - loudly, in the report, instead of silently understating a method split that finance then ties decisions to. Decide the ELSE deliberately: ELSE 0 makes non-matching rows contribute nothing to that column, which is what a partition requires; omitting ELSE yields NULL contributions that SUM happens to ignore, giving the same numbers with muddier intent. And if the method list is long or volatile, rows-not-columns (GROUP BY month, method) is the more maintainable shape - pivots earn their width only when the column set is small and stable.
Show each employee's full management chain as a path like 'Marla > Ana > Cy' - I need the chain itself, not just the depth.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, manager_id INTEGER REFERENCES employees(id))
INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1, 'Marla', NULL), (2, 'Ana', 1), (3, 'Bo', 1), (4, 'Cy', 2), (5, 'Dee', 2), (6, 'Eli', 4)

WITH RECURSIVE org(id, name, path) AS (SELECT id, name, name FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.name, o.path || ' > ' || e.name FROM employees e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id) SELECT name, path FROM org ORDER BY path

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	path
Marla	Marla
Ana	Marla > Ana
Cy	Marla > Ana > Cy
Eli	Marla > Ana > Cy > Eli
Dee	Marla > Ana > Dee
Bo	Marla > Bo

The recursive walk can carry more than a counter: here each step extends a path string, appending ' > ' and the new name to the chain built so far. Eli's row reads 'Marla > Ana > Cy > Eli' - the entire line of management above him in one glance - and the walk produces 6 paths, one per employee, with Marla's path being just her own name. Ordering by the path string itself is a quiet bonus of this representation: it sorts the chart into a readable tree order, parents immediately before their subtrees, because a child's path begins with the parent's full path as a prefix. Depth-first listings fall out of lexicographic sorting for free. The construction inherits every recursive-CTE caveat - cycles loop, so real data wants a depth guard - and adds one of its own: the separator must not appear inside names, or the path becomes ambiguous to parse back. Treat the path as a display artifact computed on read; if chains are queried often (everyone under Ana = path LIKE 'Marla > Ana > %'), materializing it as a maintained column is a legitimate denormalization, with the recursive query as its builder and validator.
Two ways to find customers who have never ordered: LEFT JOIN with IS NULL, and NOT EXISTS. A teammate swears one of them is wrong. Settle it with data.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER REFERENCES customers(id), total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'Ana'), (2, 'Bo'), (3, 'Cy'), (4, 'Dee')
SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.name
SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) ORDER BY c.name

messages.content: Your teammate is wrong - on well-formed keys the two are exactly equivalent, and both return Bo, Dee: the 2 customers with no orders. The LEFT JOIN version keeps every customer, pads non-orderers with NULL order columns, and the IS NULL filter keeps precisely the padded ones. NOT EXISTS asks the same question in the negative directly. Same set, same order, same truth. Where they genuinely diverge is at the edges of key hygiene, and knowing the edges is the real answer. If orders.customer_id could be NULL, NOT EXISTS still behaves (a NULL matches nobody, correctly), while the LEFT JOIN version also behaves - the divergence appears with the third spelling, NOT IN, which the NULL poisons into returning nobody at all. And if the join key were not the child's foreign key but some nullable attribute, the IS NULL test could misfire on a matched row whose tested column is legitimately NULL - which is why the idiom tests the child's primary key (o.id), a column that is NULL only when no child row exists. So: both correct, NOT EXISTS usually clearer in intent and easier for the optimizer to short-circuit, LEFT JOIN IS NULL handy when the query already joins for other columns. The spelling to actually fear is the one not on the table.
Total salary cost under each manager - meaning their whole subtree, not just direct reports - for budgeting the reorg.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, manager_id INTEGER REFERENCES employees(id), salary_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)

WITH RECURSIVE sub(root_id, emp_id, salary_cents) AS (SELECT id, id, salary_cents FROM employees UNION ALL SELECT s.root_id, e.id, e.salary_cents FROM sub s JOIN employees e ON e.manager_id = s.emp_id) SELECT r.name, SUM(s.salary_cents) - r.salary_cents AS subtree_cost FROM sub s JOIN employees r ON r.id = s.root_id GROUP BY r.id, r.name ORDER BY subtree_cost DESC

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	subtree_cost
Marla	42500000
Ana	21500000
Cy	6000000
Bo	0
Dee	0
Eli	0

The trick is to root a separate recursion at every employee: the anchor seeds one walk per person (each employee as their own root), and the recursive step descends from wherever the walk currently is, tagging every descendant with the root it started from. Grouping by root then sums a whole subtree in one pass. Marla's subtree - everyone - costs 42500000 cents beneath her own salary; Ana's costs 21500000; Cy's is just Eli at 6000000; and the leaf managers Bo, Dee, and Eli correctly total 0 beneath themselves. Subtracting the root's own salary is the presentation decision made explicit: 'cost under a manager' excludes the manager; include it and the same query answers 'cost of the org rooted at' instead. Say which one a budget document means before circulating either. Complexity honesty: this computes all subtrees in a single recursive walk of the anchor-per-node forest, which visits each (root, descendant) pair once - quadratic in pathological deep chains, trivial at real org sizes. It also inherits the cycle caveat: a management loop would recurse without end, so the depth guard belongs in any production version. Recursion plus a root tag turns one tree walk into every subtree answer at once - the most leverage per line in this entire batch.
